Article Title: A $25 million Boca Raton mansion now has AI running the home; inside the futuristic Florida property with 150 feet of waterfront
Article Text:
$25 million Boca Raton mansion with 150 feet of waterfront (Image Credit: Daniel Petron via realtor.com)

A waterfront home built around technology

This Boca Raton mansion blends AI, luxury and 150 feet of waterfront on Florida's coast (Image Credit: Daniel Petron via realtor.com)

Inside the $25 million mansion

A resort-style private retreat

Artificial intelligence is moving beyond phones, computers and workplaces and into some of the world's most expensive homes. A newly listed mansion in Boca Raton, Florida, offers a striking example of that shift, combining luxury waterfront living with an extensive smart-home system designed to control much of the property. According to realtor.com, the two-story residence, listed for $24.995 million, has six bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms and approximately 10,814 square feet of interior living space. The home uses Josh AI alongside Lutron, Sonos and Crestron technology to control features including lighting, window shades, sound and climate. The property also has six remotely accessible security cameras and sits along 150 feet of Intracoastal Waterway frontage.Located at 2401 Spanish River Road, the Boca Raton estate sits on nearly half an acre and underwent a major transformation in 2024. The redesign turned the property into a contemporary waterfront retreat, combining modern architecture with technology intended to make everyday life easier. The home's artificial intelligence system is one of its most unusual features. Rather than relying only on conventional switches and controls, the system allows residents to interact with the home using voice commands.Josh AI works alongside other smart-home technologies to manage different parts of the property.Lighting, window shades, audio and climate controls can all be integrated into the system. Security is also connected, with six cameras that can be monitored remotely. The idea is to allow the technology to operate quietly in the background while residents control the home's environment with minimal effort. But despite its high-tech systems, the property is designed to feel more like a luxury resort than a futuristic laboratory.The home's 2024 redesign was overseen by Umber Architecture, with interiors by Eric Dyer of Arthur Collection and construction by BNK Construction. The design combines pale stone, warm wood and large areas of glass, creating interiors that emphasise the waterfront setting. Ten-foot ceilings run through the main floor, while marmorino plaster adds texture to the walls. A custom staircase with stone treads serves as an architectural focal point as visitors move through the main entertaining areas.According to realtor.com, the home features a spacious 44-by-29-foot great room and a separate living room that extends more than 32 feet in length. The dining room covers roughly 21 by 20 feet, providing substantial space for entertaining. The kitchen, approximately 30 feet long, is another major feature. It is centred around Brazilian Casablanca quartzite and includes integrated Miele and Sub-Zero appliances. Custom cabinetry allows parts of the kitchen to be concealed when not in use, helping maintain the clean appearance of the room. There is also a second kitchen for preparation, along with a wine room capable of holding 214 bottles. An elevator, wet bar, custom closets and an air-conditioned three-car garage add to the home's amenities.Upstairs, the primary suite continues the home's hotel-inspired design. The bedroom features custom woodwork, a sitting area and a balcony overlooking the Intracoastal Waterway. Its bathroom uses Belvedere quartzite and includes a steam shower, soaking tub, vanity and a large dressing area. Five additional bedrooms are spread throughout the house, including one on the main level.Outside, the property is designed for entertaining as much as relaxing. The backyard features a heated saltwater swimming pool, covered loggia, pergola, summer kitchen and built-in barbecue. Multiple patios, terraces, balconies and a deck provide different areas for enjoying the gardens and waterfront views. The landscaping includes California olive trees, while the property also has a private dock and ocean access. Both the seawall and dock were completed in 2024. Additional systems include a generator, tankless water heater and water purification system.With its combination of waterfront access, resort-style interiors and AI-assisted home controls, the Boca Raton property reflects how technology is becoming part of the luxury-home experience. For a buyer willing to spend nearly $25 million, the appeal is not simply having a smart home, but having a residence where many everyday functions can be managed through an integrated system, while the architecture and waterfront setting remain central to the property's appeal.
Article Summary: Boca Raton mansion has six bedrooms, 6.5 bathrooms and 10,814 square feet of interior living space. Home uses Josh AI alongside Lutron, Sonos and Crestron technology to control features including lighting, window shades, sound and climate. Property also has six remotely accessible security cameras and sits along 150 feet of waterfront.

Article Title: Brazil's Porto Seguro is paying $10 for each captured lionfish; nearly 500 have been removed as they threaten native reefs and local fisheries
Article Text:
Alert for invasion

The alert in Porto Seguro intensified on June 12, 2026, when the first official occurrence of the lionfish was recorded in the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park.

Spreading across the region

In August 2026, the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation or ICMBio, confirmed lionfish in the Abrolhos Marine National Park

The municipality of Porto Seguro, Brazil, is paying $10 for each captured lionfish, which has invaded the region's waters and threatened native species. Nearly 500 of the invasive fish have been removed from the sea far south of Bahia, in about a month after the invasion, and brought to the Fishermen's Colony in areas outside of the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park. Authorities are attempting to control a venomous predator that reproduces rapidly, threatening local reefs, native fish, crustaceans and fisheries, according to a report by CPG.Lionfish are native to the Indo-Pacific and have found favourable conditions to spread throughout the Atlantic Ocean. Combined with their high reproductive capacity and few natural control mechanisms, they have further invaded areas that support their expansion. Moreover, they do not have a specific diet. They can consume various marine organisms, including small fish, crustaceans and other prey. They are also not restricted to a specific habitat and can occupy reefs, rocky areas, mangroves and other marine environments.Not just aquatic members, they also pose a risk to people who come into contact with the fish. An adult lionfish can have up to 18 venomous spines distributed across its fins that function as a defence mechanism.If someone touches, steps on or attempts to handle them, their sting can lead to intense pain and nausea.In 2022, the Department of Health of Ceará recorded a case involving a 24-year-old fisherman. The fisherman stepped on a lionfish and suffered seven stings to the foot, leading to intense pain, fever and convulsions.The alert in Porto Seguro intensified on June 12, 2026, when the first official occurrence of the lionfish was recorded in the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park. Shortly after, new specimens began to appear, prompting local authorities to expand their response. Now, lionfish are being captured for $10 each in an operation involving local fishermen and the Municipal Department of Environment and Animal Causes, known as Semac. The measure is temporary and is part of actions directed at areas outside the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park.The strategy is aimed at curbing the numbers before the species is widely established in the area. According to sources, the sooner an invasive species is identified and controlled, the greater are the chances of reducing its impacts. Porto Seguro has developed a Municipal Action Plan to tackle lionfish. The document encompasses measures for monitoring, capture, scientific research, training, and accident prevention.The specimens are not just being removed but also being used as scientific material. The priority is to send them to the Marine Ecology and Conservation Laboratory of the Federal University of Southern Bahia, Lecomar/UFSB. In the laboratory, the animals can be weighed, measured, and analysed.The analyses seek to understand how the invasion is establishing itself along the Bahia coastline. Researchers are investigating diet, genetics, origin, behaviour, and distribution of the captured fish. This information helps identify where the species is concentrating and which native organisms appear in its diet.Surprisingly, the presence of this species is not restricted to Porto Seguro. In August 2026, the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation or ICMBio, confirmed lionfish in the Abrolhos Marine National Park, also along the Bahia coastline. The area is home to significant biodiversity and South Atlantic coral reef formations.Following the record in Abrolhos, ICMBio reported that it began taking action in partnership with other institutions. The actions include monitoring and management of the species, given the concern over the lionfish’s ability to continue advancing along the Brazilian coast.
Article Summary: The municipality of Porto Seguro, Brazil, is paying $10 for each captured lionfish, which has invaded the region's waters. Nearly 500 of the invasive fish have been removed from the sea far south of Bahia, in about a month after the invasion. Authorities are attempting to control a venomous predator that reproduces rapidly.

Article Title: San Diego high school students created 39 wildlife gardens in just 4 years; now nearly 25,000 sq ft of habitat supports native plants and pollinators
Article Text:
How San Diego students created 39 wildlife gardens

Nearly 25,000 sq ft of habitat restored

Native plants support pollinators

Students transformed unused spaces

The project expanded beyond school campuses

San Diego schools increased native plant options

The programme has grown since 2022

Students are learning about conservation careers

A four-year effort that continues to grow

Nearly 350 San Diego high-school students have spent the past four years turning school grounds and community spaces into native wildlife gardens, helping create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens. The work is part of the Native Biodiversity Corps, a San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance programme launched in 2022 to give students hands-on experience in conservation. Participants learn about native plants, wildlife and habitat restoration before designing, planting and maintaining gardens with guidance from conservation professionals. The gardens are intended to provide resources for pollinators and other local wildlife in urban areas while giving students practical conservation skills. The programme has also expanded beyond schools, with students helping transform an unused golf-course space into a native garden.The Native Biodiversity Corps began in spring 2022 with funding from San Diego's Level Up programme. More than 300 urban high-school students registered within 72 hours, while about 100 students were selected for the inaugural programme. Participants spent the summer visiting conservation sites including the San Diego Zoo, San Diego Zoo Safari Park, San Diego Natural History Museum, Living Coast Discovery Center and San Elijo Lagoon Ecological Reserve.They then used what they had learned to design and build native wildlife gardens at Crawford, Hoover and Lincoln high schools.Students are involved in more than simply planting vegetation. They survey potential garden locations, develop designs, select suitable native plants, help implement the projects and participate in maintaining the gardens. The programme gives them an opportunity to learn about local ecosystems while working alongside conservation professionals and applying ecological concepts in real-world settings.According to San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance's September 2026 update, nearly 350 students have participated in the Native Biodiversity Corps since its launch. Together, they have helped create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens on school grounds and elsewhere across San Diego County.The figure represents the combined area of multiple gardens rather than one continuous wildlife reserve. The projects vary in size and location, but they share an emphasis on using native vegetation to create habitat and ecological resources within developed areas.A central aim of the gardens is to provide food and habitat for pollinators and other wildlife. At Hoover High School, students transformed a tree planter into a pollinator garden containing California poppy, narrowleaf milkweed, showy penstemon and California buckwheat.The use of native plants is important because they are adapted to the region's environmental conditions and can provide resources for species that have evolved alongside them. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says the gardens can also contribute to habitat corridors, creating a network of smaller green spaces that can provide resources for wildlife moving through urban areas.Some of the projects have involved spaces that previously provided little habitat. At Crawford High School, students transformed an undeveloped hillside into a green space. At another location, students created a native garden on a previously bare hillside, with the goal of providing habitat resources for local pollinators.The projects give students direct responsibility for changing their surroundings. Instead of learning about biodiversity solely through textbooks, they can observe how plants develop and how wildlife responds as the gardens mature.The students' conservation work has increasingly moved into wider community spaces. In one project, Native Biodiversity Corps participants worked with Pro Kids, First Tee to transform an unused chipping range at Colina Park Golf Course into a waterwise native garden containing 27 different native plant species.During the 2026 summer programme, students also worked with the San Diego Zoo Safari Park's horticulture team to design and install a native wildlife garden at the Beckman Center for Conservation Research. These projects have allowed students to take the skills learned at school and apply them to larger community and conservation settings.The programme has also contributed to changes in school landscaping. When the initiative began, San Diego Unified School District had four native plant species approved for use on its campuses, according to the Zoo Wildlife Alliance. Through collaboration involving students, teachers, administrators and conservation specialists, that number has grown to nearly 30 native plant species.The development means the programme's influence has extended beyond individual gardens. Students have been involved in a broader effort to increase the use of native vegetation across school environments.The latest figures show how quickly the initiative has expanded. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance's 2024 annual report recorded 60 Native Biodiversity Corps students from three partner high schools, who designed and planted native gardens and helped create or restore more than 8,600 square feet of native wildlife habitat through 18 gardens.Its 2025 annual report subsequently recorded 180 students creating 10 native gardens during that reporting period. Students also participated in other conservation activities, including distributing native seedlings, supporting butterfly conservation and planting 10 trees with San Diego's Urban Forestry team.The latest September 2026 update puts the cumulative programme totals at nearly 350 students, 39 gardens and almost 25,000 square feet of created or restored habitat.The programme is designed to provide students with more than gardening experience. Participants work with conservation scientists, horticulturists and other specialists, giving them exposure to careers involving wildlife, plants, habitat restoration and environmental education.One participant, Gabi, joined the programme during its inaugural year and continued through 2026 before going to college to study landscape architecture. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says other students have also developed an interest in conservation and environmental careers as a result of their experience.The programme also provides financial recognition for students' work. According to the Zoo Wildlife Alliance, students who successfully complete a session and maintain active participation can be eligible for stipends of up to $2,000.This allows students to gain practical conservation experience while receiving support for the time they commit to the programme.San Diego County is recognised for its exceptional biodiversity, but urban development has fragmented many natural habitats. Native gardens cannot replace large protected ecosystems, but they can provide smaller patches of vegetation and resources within developed landscapes. The Native Biodiversity Corps uses school campuses and community spaces to create these pockets of native habitat. The Zoo Wildlife Alliance says the network of gardens can help provide resources for pollinators and other wildlife and potentially contribute to habitat connectivity across urban areas.What began in 2022 as a conservation programme for high-school students has developed into a county-wide initiative involving nearly 350 young people. In four years, participants have helped create or restore almost 25,000 square feet of habitat through 39 gardens, while gaining practical experience in native planting, habitat restoration and biodiversity conservation.The programme's impact therefore extends beyond the gardens themselves. Students leave behind native plantings that can be maintained by future cohorts while carrying conservation knowledge into their further education and careers. The result is a growing network of small habitat patches created by students who began the programme by learning about biodiversity and ended up helping put those lessons into practice.
Article Summary: San Diego high-school students have spent the past four years turning school grounds and community spaces into native wildlife gardens. The work is part of the Native Biodiversity Corps, a San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance programme launched in 2022. Participants learn about native plants, wildlife and habitat restoration before designing, planting and maintaining gardens.

Article Title: Scientists reconstructed a Wyoming forest from 56-million-year-old fossil leaves; it lost about 60% of its canopy during ancient warming and took more than 100,000 years to recover
Article Text:
Wyoming tetons Representative image from Canva

A forest preserved in stone

Reconstructing the forest from thousands of leaves

What the leaves revealed about the warming event

A long, slow recovery

Why this matters for today’s forests

What the study adds to our understanding

A cautionary tale written in leaves

Deep in the rock record of Wyoming, a layer of fossil leaves tells a quiet but powerful story about what happens to forests when the planet warms rapidly. About 56 million years ago, during a spike in global temperatures known as the Paleocene Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM), a lush subtropical forest that once covered the region lost roughly 60 percent of its canopy. New research titled 'Forest canopy decline under elevated CO2 during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum' published in the journal Science, based on tens of thousands of fossil leaves, shows that the ecosystem did not bounce back quickly. It took more than 100,000 years for the forest to regain its former diversity and structure. As reported by Smithsonian Magazine, the findings offer a rare, detailed look at how ancient forests responded to extreme warming and provide a sobering parallel for today’s climate change.The story begins in the Bighorn Basin of north central Wyoming, where sedimentary rocks from the early Eocene epoch are rich in plant fossils. Over millions of years, leaves that fell into ancient rivers and floodplains were buried in fine mud and sand. They left detailed impressions, even preserving the tiny veins and edges botanists use to identify species, under the right conditions.Paleobotanists have collected these fossil leaves for decades in an effort to reconstruct past climates and ecosystems. Scientists can work out how hot or wet it was and what the forests looked like by counting species, measuring leaf shapes and analyzing their traits. The Wyoming sites are especially valuable because they span the time before, during and after the Paleocene Eocene Thermal Maximum, or PETM, a short but intense warming event that pushed global temperatures up by several degrees in a geologic instant.In the new study, researchers assembled a massive dataset of fossil leaves from multiple sites in the Bighorn Basin. They examined tens of thousands of specimens, identifying plant species and categorising them by traits such as leaf size, shape and margin type. These traits are linked to how plants cope with temperature, water availability and light, so they serve as proxies for the structure and health of the forest.By comparing the leaves that existed before the PETM, at its peak and in the thousands of years after, the team could trace how the forest changed through time. They examined the number of species present, the dominance of certain plant types and the changes in overall canopy structure as the climate warmed and then cooled slowly.Before the PETM, the Wyoming forest was diverse and dense, with a multi layered canopy of broadleaf trees and a rich understory. The fossil leaves include many species, many of which have characteristics that would have been good for warm, wet conditions. This was a lush subtropical ecosystem, similar in some respects to some modern forests in parts of East Asia or the southeastern United States.As the PETM unfolded, the fossil record changes dramatically. The number of species drops sharply. Many of the large, broad leaves that indicate a closed, shady canopy become rare. Instead, the fossil assemblages are dominated by a smaller set of species with traits suited to hotter, drier and more open conditions. Based on these shifts, the researchers estimate that the forest lost about 60 percent of its canopy cover during the height of the warming.In practical terms, this means that large swaths of what had been dense forest became more like open woodland or scrub. Sunlight reached the ground more easily, temperatures at the surface rose and the microclimates that many plants and animals depended on were disrupted.One of the most striking findings is how long it took the forest to recover. After the PETM peaked, global temperatures gradually declined over tens of thousands of years. But the Wyoming forest did not quickly return to its pre warming state. The fossil leaves show that low diversity and reduced canopy cover persisted for a very long time.It took more than 100,000 years for the forest to regain much of its original species richness and structural complexity. Even then, the mix of plants was not identical to what had existed before. Some species never returned, while others that had been rare became more common. The ecosystem that emerged after the PETM was related to the original forest but not the same.This slow recovery highlights a key point. Even when temperatures eventually come down, the biological impacts of rapid warming can last far longer than the warming itself. Forests do not simply flip back to their previous state once the climate stabilises. They must reassemble through colonisation, competition and evolution, processes that operate on much longer time scales.The PETM is not a perfect analog for modern climate change. The causes were different, involving massive releases of carbon from volcanic activity and possibly methane from seafloor sediments, rather than human burning of fossil fuels. The rate of warming, while rapid in geologic terms, was still slower than what humans are driving today. But the basic lesson is relevant. When the climate shifts quickly, forests can lose a large portion of their canopy and diversity, and they may not recover within time frames that matter for human societies.Today’s forests already face multiple stresses, including logging, land conversion, invasive species and fragmentation. Adding rapid warming on top of these pressures could push some ecosystems past tipping points where recovery becomes difficult or impossible within centuries. The Wyoming fossil record suggests that even without human land use, a forest can take more than 100,000 years to regain what it lost during a relatively short warming spike.Previous work on the PETM has shown that many plant and animal groups were affected, but the Wyoming leaf dataset provides unusual detail. It allows scientists to quantify changes in canopy cover and diversity with a resolution that is rare in the fossil record. The study moves beyond general statements that forests were stressed to specific estimates of how much canopy was lost and how long recovery took.This level of detail helps climate modelers and ecologists test ideas about how forests respond to warming. It also gives conservationists a long term perspective on what might lie ahead if current emissions continue. The message is not that every forest will collapse, but that large-scale losses and long recovery times are well within the realm of possibility based on past events.The fossil leaves of the Bighorn Basin are more than scientific specimens. They are pages in a very old story about climate, ecosystems and resilience. They show that forests can endure extreme warming, but at a cost. They can lose much of their canopy, shed species and become simpler, sunnier places for thousands of generations.For people living today, the time scales involved are hard to grasp. A recovery period of more than 100,000 years is far longer than human civilisation has existed. It is a reminder that some changes set in motion now may not be fully reversible within any time frame that matters for our descendants.The Wyoming forest did eventually grow back, but not quickly and not exactly as it was. The fossil leaves preserved in its rocks offer a clear warning. How we manage warming in the coming decades will shape the world’s forests not just for our lifetimes, but for many millennia to come.
Article Summary: Fossil leaves from the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming reveal how forests changed during the Paleocene Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) It took more than 100,000 years for the forest to regain its former diversity and structure. The findings offer a rare, detailed look at how ancient forests responded to extreme warming and provide a sobering parallel for today's climate change.

Article Title: In 1953, North and South Korea established a demilitarised zone; decades later human isolation led to the formation of a 155-mile-long wildlife haven
Article Text:
A wildlife haven

Conservation efforts

Eco-tourism

Soldiers on both sides stand behind fences and in between are thousands of landmines. For more than 70 years, humans have not ventured into a 155-mile-long corridor that divides two nations, North and South Korea. While boundaries and borders can ward people off, nature is above all such regulations. This is probably why a space where beings seldom step in has transformed into a surprising wildlife haven for flora and fauna.The Korean Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) was created by the armistice that halted the Korean War in 1953. To date, it remains surrounded by soldiers, fences, watchtowers and landmines, making it one of the most fortified and militarised borders in the world. For humans, it is among the most forbidden places on Earth, but for wildlife it is a home they return to.DMZ extends about 155 miles across the Korean Peninsula and is about 2.5 miles wide. It covers everything 2 kilometres north and south of the border between the two countries. Since civilian access to the area is severely restricted, it has escaped the trenches of roads, buildings and intensive farming found elsewhere.According to surveys, in the past seven decades, 6,168 species have been identified in the area in and around the DMZ, according to a report by AS. 38% (102) of the South Korean Peninsula's 267 endangered species have been recorded there. This list includes musk deer, leopards, long-tailed gorals and Asiatic black bears. Otters are known to travel along the rivers without recognising the intense political divide. Remote cameras have even captured a young black bear, providing evidence that the animals may be breeding there.But the most striking residents of the area are found in the air. Seven of the world's fifteen crane species have been seen in the region, including the endangered red-crowned and white-naped cranes. According to the DMZ Ecology Research Institute, while wetlands in China and Japan are disappearing, the DMZ offers a peaceful sanctuary for these migratory birds. As wetlands have disappeared elsewhere in East Asia, the rice paddies and marshes near the border have become invaluable stopping places.“The demilitarised zone is a symbol of hope. It shows everything can be restored,” Seung-ho Kim, Director of the DMZ Ecology Research Institute, told Earth.Org.Even though human access to the area is severely restricted, numerous Korean organisations are involved in the conservation and preservation of the DMZ and its inhabitants. “For the past 30 years, Green Korea United has conducted extensive on-the-ground surveys across the Civilian Control Zone and border areas to monitor the habitats of endangered wildlife,” said Dasom Lee, Director of the Ecosystem Conservation Team of Green Korea United (GKU).The accumulated area from the surveys helped GKU successfully advocate for the designation of 70,000 hectares of land in the DMZ buffer zones as protected areas. "The preservation of the Civilian Control Zone south of the DMZ over the past 70 years is the result of both legal environmental protection and the restriction of human access due to military constraints,” Lee told Earth.Org.Pictures taken by unmanned eco cameras installed by the National Institute of Ecology offer a glimpse of the wildlife in the isolated area. Field research can only be done in the Civilian Control Zone (CCZ), a buffer area south of the DMZ. While public access is also heavily restricted here, a limited number of people are allowed to enter, and even farm, within the CCZ area. The agricultural land is mainly used to grow rice.Every week, Seung-ho Kim, Director of the DMZ Ecology Research Institute and volunteers from the institute enter the CCZ to conduct field research. “Interestingly, the small waterways of the rice paddies are home to the most endangered species. The paddies are very different from the rice fields outside the CCZ; they contain more weeds and are very traditional,” said Kim, who started the research centre in 2004 to preserve and protect the area through research and educational activities.“We are testing microhabitats which can function as corridors to bring more wildlife. For example, the weeds in rice paddies could function as a corridor for deer, leopard cats or birds. This year, we are also testing rock piles to see how they function as a microhabitat for small mammals such as mice, reptiles, and snakes,” he explained.The uniqueness of the area, its ecological value and the wildlife it inhabits have gained attention worldwide. The presence of rare migratory birds has led to the development of bird-watching tours in the area. The South Korean government developed the DMZ Peace Trail to help restore tourism in the border regions and to boost the local economy.Those who want to walk one of the 11 routes need to go through an identification verification process and can enter the area in small groups guided by local tour guides. To protect the environment, only small parts of the route can be walked; the rest can be visited by bus.
Article Summary: The Korean Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) was created by the armistice that halted the Korean War in 1953. It remains surrounded by soldiers, fences, watchtowers and landmines, making it one of the most fortified and militarised borders in the world. For humans, it is among the most forbidden places on Earth, but for wildlife it is a home they return to. 38% of the South Korean Peninsula's 267 endangered species have been recorded there. Remote cameras have even captured a young black bear.

Article Title: A farmer turned 70 acres of his Oregon barley farm into a wetland; now it hosts 140 bird species and endangered fish
Article Text:
Image: JPR/OPB

Why an Oregon farmer turned 70 acres of his barley farm into a wetland

Why an Oregon farmer turned 70 acres of his barley farm into a wetland

Plant diversity also increased

The wetland became a refuge for endangered fish

Thousands of young suckers were introduced

Researchers found 50 adult-sized fish

The wetland also helps clean agricultural water

A different model for farmland restoration

A project built on collaboration

The wider Klamath Basin challenge

A small farm experiment with a bigger possibility

A farmer in southern Oregon transformed 70 acres of his 400-acre barley farm into a wetland in 2021, creating an unexpected refuge for wildlife while helping address agricultural water pollution. Karl Wenner, a co-owner of Lakeside Farms near Klamath Falls, worked with conservation agencies and other partners to convert flood-prone farmland into a managed wetland. The area now attracts tens of thousands of ducks, geese and swans and supports at least 140 bird species, along with otters, beavers and muskrats. More significantly, the wetland has been used to raise federally endangered Lost River and shortnose suckers. In 2025, researchers found 50 adult-sized suckers after partially draining the wetland, offering a promising sign for species struggling with poor juvenile survival.Wenner became a co-owner of Lakeside Farms in 2017. The roughly 400-acre property had traditionally been used to grow barley and sits near Upper Klamath Lake, an important wetland and waterbird habitat in southern Oregon. Wenner initially appreciated the farm because its abundant water attracted ducks, but he later became concerned about the quality of water leaving the agricultural land.Tests showed that the water carried high concentrations of phosphorus, a nutrient that can contribute to harmful algal blooms in Upper Klamath Lake. Instead of continuing to farm the most flood-prone portion of the property, Wenner and his partners explored whether the land could be used to naturally filter agricultural runoff while providing wildlife habitat.The restoration project began taking shape in 2021, when about 70 acres of the farm were converted into a semi-permanent wetland. The area was engineered with shallow water areas, channels, dikes and islands that allow water to move slowly through the site. Rather than flowing directly towards Upper Klamath Lake, agricultural water can pass through the wetland, where vegetation and sediments capture nutrients and suspended material. The project was designed to provide environmental benefits without requiring the entire farm to be taken out of agricultural production. The remaining land continues to be used for farming, making the project an example of how restoration and agriculture can operate alongside each other.Wildlife responded quickly after the wetland was established. US Fish and Wildlife Service records documented more than 20,000 ducks using the property during October and November. Later reporting found that the restored area had attracted tens of thousands of ducks, geese and swans, while at least 140 bird species had been recorded at the farm. The wetland also became home to other wildlife, including otters, beavers and muskrats. Its rapid development into a productive habitat is particularly notable because the area had previously been used primarily as agricultural land.The ecological changes were not limited to birds and mammals. Researchers used pollen collected by bees to study plant diversity around the farm. The analysis indicated that plant biodiversity had doubled within two years of the wetland restoration. Bee-based monitoring also helped identify native plants growing around the property and highlighted invasive species that could be targeted for removal. The approach gave researchers another way to measure how the landscape was changing as agricultural fields were replaced, at least partly, by wetland habitat.The project also took on significance for two endangered fish species found in the Klamath Basin. The Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker are both federally listed as endangered and are culturally important to the Klamath Tribes. Their populations have declined dramatically, with poor survival of young fish contributing to the difficulty of rebuilding their numbers. Conservationists therefore need places where juvenile suckers can survive and grow before eventually joining the wider lake population. Parts of the Lakeside Farms property were modified to provide such habitat, creating a protected environment that could serve as a nursery for the fish.As part of the conservation work, young suckers were introduced into ponds on the farm. Different releases and accounts have recorded varying numbers, with the broader project involving several thousand juvenile fish. The fish included endangered Lost River and shortnose suckers as well as native Klamath largescale suckers. The aim was not simply to increase the number of fish on the farm but to determine whether restored wetland conditions could allow young suckers to survive and develop in an environment resembling the shallow habitats that historically existed around Upper Klamath Lake.A particularly significant development came in May 2025, when researchers partially drained the wetland to assess how the stocked fish had fared. They found 50 adult-sized suckers, with some measuring up to about 16 inches. The recovered fish appeared healthy and had reached a size comparable with mature fish. Researchers cautioned that the sampling might not have captured every fish in the wetland and that genetic testing was needed to determine the precise species composition of the recovered fish. The discovery nevertheless provided evidence that at least some stocked suckers had survived and grown substantially in the restored habitat.The discovery is important because the Klamath Basin's sucker populations face a serious recruitment problem. Many young fish fail to survive long enough to become adults, leaving existing populations dominated by older fish. Poor water quality, habitat loss, altered water flows and other environmental pressures have contributed to the decline. The Lakeside Farms project does not solve those wider problems, nor does the discovery of 50 adult-sized fish prove that a self-sustaining population has been established. It does, however, suggest that restored wetlands on working agricultural land could provide valuable rearing habitat for young suckers.Wildlife restoration was only part of the project's purpose. The wetland was also designed to improve the quality of water leaving the farm. Excess phosphorus entering Upper Klamath Lake can contribute to nutrient pollution and harmful algal blooms, which can create difficult conditions for aquatic life. By slowing water and allowing plants and sediments to absorb or retain nutrients, the wetland acts as a natural treatment system before water reaches the lake. Reports on the project indicate that phosphorus levels in water leaving the wetland were substantially reduced, demonstrating how agricultural land can potentially be used to address some of the environmental impacts associated with farming.The project has attracted attention because the land has not simply been permanently removed from agriculture. Some fields can be managed as wetlands for periods before potentially returning to crop production. Flooding can also help suppress weeds and pests and may improve soil conditions. Wenner and his partners have therefore been testing whether farmers can receive ecological benefits while retaining an economically viable agricultural operation. Other landowners in the Klamath Basin have reportedly shown interest in similar approaches, suggesting that the experiment could eventually be replicated elsewhere.The transformation was not carried out by Wenner alone. Lakeside Farms worked with federal and local conservation organisations, including the US Fish and Wildlife Service and Klamath Watershed Partnership. Funding and technical support helped with the wetland's design, construction and ongoing management. The project also brought agricultural interests into closer contact with conservation efforts involving the Klamath Tribes and endangered sucker recovery. That collaboration is significant in a region where disputes over water, farming and endangered species have persisted for decades.The significance of the farm becomes clearer when viewed against the history of the Klamath Basin. Large areas of the region's historic wetlands have been lost or altered, while agriculture has changed the way water moves through the landscape. Upper Klamath Lake remains an important habitat for migratory birds but also faces persistent water-quality challenges. The two endangered sucker species have suffered severe population declines, making the creation of additional shallow-water habitat particularly valuable. Against that backdrop, a 70-acre wetland may be relatively small, but it offers a practical demonstration of how individual farms can contribute to broader restoration efforts.The Lakeside Farms project began with a relatively simple question about what to do with flood-prone farmland and polluted agricultural water. Four years after the wetland was created, the results had extended far beyond water treatment. Tens of thousands of waterfowl were using the property, at least 140 bird species had been recorded, plant diversity had increased and endangered suckers had survived to adult size. The project is not a complete solution to the Klamath Basin's environmental problems, but it demonstrates how a working farm can be redesigned to provide food, habitat and cleaner water at the same time.
Article Summary: A farmer in southern Oregon transformed 70 acres of his 400-acre barley farm into a wetland in 2021. The area now attracts tens of thousands of ducks, geese and swans and supports at least 140 bird species. The wetland has been used to raise federally endangered Lost River and shortnose suckers. In 2025, researchers found 50 adult-sized suckers after partially draining the wetland.

Article Title: In 1963, Rat Pack composer Jimmy Van Heusen bought a secluded California mountain; decades later it became a legendary celebrity hideaway
Article Text:
Image(s): Left/Jimmy Van Heusen and Sammy Cahn/American Songwriter/Right/Rattlesnake Ranch

Why Jimmy Van Heusen escaped Hollywood for Yucca Valley

The secluded mountain became a Rat Pack escape

The secluded mountain became a Rat Pack escape (Image: Rattlesnake Ranch)

The JFK and Marilyn Monroe story has a catch

Van Heusen eventually left, and the ranch fell into disrepair

Rattlesnake Ranch is being reborn as a luxury desert retreat

Some places become famous because of what they look like, and then there are places whose reputation comes almost entirely from the people who once gathered there. High above Yucca Valley in California’s high desert, Rattlesnake Ranch belongs firmly to the second category. Composer Jimmy Van Heusen bought the secluded mountaintop in 1963, seeking the privacy that increasingly eluded Hollywood stars in nearby Palm Springs. What followed was a remarkable chapter in Rat Pack history, as the retreat became associated with Van Heusen’s close friends Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby, as well as visits from President John F. Kennedy. Today, after years of decline, the once-secret hideaway is being restored as a luxury rental, giving a new generation a glimpse into one of Hollywood’s most colourful desert escapes.Van Heusen was far more than a composer living in the shadow of the stars he wrote for. A four-time Oscar winner, he created enduring songs including Come Fly with Me, Call Me Irresponsible and All the Way. According to the data on the official site, his professional and personal friendship with Frank Sinatra placed him firmly inside the world that would become synonymous with the Rat Pack. By the early 1960s, however, Palm Springs no longer offered the isolation that celebrities wanted.The desert resort had become so popular with Hollywood figures and tourists that privacy was increasingly difficult to find. Van Heusen went further into the high desert and chose a mountain overlooking Yucca Valley. The finished retreat became known variously as Scenic Mountain, JVH Ranch and, eventually, Rattlesnake Ranch. The setting was almost perfectly suited to the lifestyle Van Heusen had cultivated, isolated, difficult to stumble upon, and far removed from Hollywood's watchful eyes.Rattlesnake Ranch soon developed a reputation considerably larger than its remote location. Sinatra was among Van Heusen's closest friends and collaborators, and the mountain became one of the places where members of the Hollywood set could disappear from public view. SFGATE visited the property during its restoration and describes the ranch as a place where Sinatra, Crosby and Kennedy were among the famous guests. The atmosphere was tied closely to the excesses associated with the Rat Pack era, with Van Heusen embracing a famously hard-living bachelor lifestyle. The ranch's isolation was part of its attraction. Unlike Palm Springs, no neighbouring homes were crowding the mountain. Guests could arrive, stay and party away from the photographers and Hollywood insiders who surrounded celebrities elsewhere. Van Heusen's connection to Sinatra was particularly important. His songs helped define the singer's catalogue, while Sinatra's former valet George Jacobs later portrayed Van Heusen as an influential figure in the singer's lifestyle as well as his professional circle. The composer became such a character in Yucca Valley that locals embraced him, and he was named honorary mayor in 1967, with actor Henry Fonda reportedly attending the ceremony.Perhaps the most enduring legend attached to Rattlesnake Ranch involves John F. Kennedy and Marilyn Monroe. The story has long suggested that the president and Monroe had an encounter at the secluded property. Both had genuine connections to Van Heusen. His song High Hopes became Kennedy's 1960 campaign song, while Van Heusen composed music for Monroe's film Let's Make Love. Kennedy also definitely visited Van Heusen's Yucca Valley home, according to contemporary reports. But one crucial detail makes the famous story difficult to accept, Monroe died in 1962, while the house was not completed until 1963. The better-documented links between Kennedy and Monroe point elsewhere in the Palm Springs area. That has not stopped the legend from becoming part of the ranch's identity. The restored pool house now includes a bedroom inspired by Monroe, while another room pays tribute to Sinatra. The property effectively preserves both the history and mythology surrounding its most famous visitors.The party years did not last forever. Van Heusen married Bobbe Brock in 1969, and the composer subsequently described a much quieter married life. He eventually sold his mountaintop retreat and returned to the Palm Springs area. The property later operated as the Scenic Mountain Club, including a restaurant, before eventually closing. For years, Rattlesnake Ranch sat largely abandoned. Thomas Cribb bought the property in 2006. By then, the main house was already in an uninhabitable condition, but the extraordinary views and complete privacy of the mountain convinced him that the place could have another life. Even in its rougher state, the property retained its pull. The pool house had been rented to visitors, and according to Cribb, it was booked more than 300 nights a year despite its rustic condition.The latest chapter is transforming the old celebrity hideaway into a carefully restored luxury property. The renovated pool house contains two bedrooms and two bathrooms and sleeps up to six people. Its design combines contemporary comforts with mid-century influences and archival photographs from Van Heusen's era. The original pool and barbecue pit have been retained, while the grounds now include a stone hot tub, sunken fire pit and a two-person swing overlooking Yucca Valley. The restoration is also deliberately preserving details that connect visitors to the ranch's past. According to the developers, the pool where Sinatra and Kennedy reportedly swam remains in place, allowing the property to retain physical links to its celebrity history. The main house is planned for a larger restoration, with four bedrooms and the return of Van Heusen's distinctive pink hot tub in the living room.Once completed, the entire mountain is expected to operate as a single rental for private stays, weddings and events. There is also a striking reminder of just how seriously Kennedy's security was taken. The property has two helicopter landing areas, with the second reportedly added after the Secret Service considered the original landing arrangement unsuitable. The main house also contained an extraordinary 37 telephone lines for the presidential visits. What remains at Rattlesnake Ranch, then, is more than an old Hollywood house. It is a physical reminder of an era when composers, singers, actors and political leaders could retreat into the desert and temporarily create a private world of their own. As the ranch moves from abandoned hideaway to restored luxury retreat, its greatest selling point remains unchanged from 1963, an entire mountain, far from everyone else.
Article Summary: Rattlesnake Ranch is being reborn as a luxury desert retreat. The secluded mountain became a Rat Pack escape in the 1960s. Composer Jimmy Van Heusen bought the secluded mountaintop in 1963. The retreat became associated with his close friends Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby, as well as visits from President John F. Kennedy.

Article Title: Nepal marks the 13th day of mourning after deadly flash floods
Article Text:
Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods.

Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods, as the country paid tribute to more than 1,355 people killed in one of its deadliest natural disasters in recent history.Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 589 foreign nationals, following the flash floods that struck Rasuwa, a district bordering China, and neighbouring areas on August 26.The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayas, unleashing powerful floodwaters that caused widespread loss of life and extensive damage to infrastructure across northern and central Nepal.According to the PTI report, Nepal has declared September 7 a national day of mourning to honour victims of the devastating floods that swept through Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other areas along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.The observance falls on the 13th day after the disaster, reflecting the traditional Hindu practice of marking the thirteenth day following a death. In many Hindu communities, the day is considered highly significant to honor the deceased members and the also mark the conclusion of the formal mourning period.The Ministry of Home Affairs said the national flag would be flown at half-mast at government offices across Nepal as well as at Nepali diplomatic missions abroad.The floods caused widespread loss of life and severe damage to homes and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges, hydropower projects and government buildings.Search and rescue operations remain underway in the hardest-hit areas, including tunnels at hydropower projects, as security personnel and specialised international rescue teams continue efforts to locate missing people and recover bodies.At least 32,000 families have been displaced, while around 7,500 homes were completely destroyed. The disaster has also disrupted livelihoods and damaged essential infrastructure across central Nepal.The government has deployed the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and other agencies to carry out search, rescue, relief and recovery operations.Specialist teams from neighbouring countries, including India, have joined the rescue efforts, particularly operations to save people believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels.Meanwhile, the Nepal government has declared Tuesday, September 8, a public holiday to commemorate Gen Z Martyrs’ Day, marking a year since the youth-led protests that reshaped the country’s political landscape.The protests erupted in Kathmandu on the same day last year after the government banned several social media platforms. Demonstrators also took to the streets over alleged corruption and what they described as the lavish lifestyles of the children of powerful politicians and government officials.The protests intensified after security forces opened fire near the Parliament building, killing 72 people, including children. The escalating unrest eventually prompted then-Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli to resign.The political fallout resulted in the dissolution of Parliament and the collapse of the coalition government led by the CPN-UML and Nepali Congress. A caretaker administration was subsequently installed, paving the way for fresh parliamentary elections on March 5 this year.The election brought the Gen Z-backed Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), led by Rabi Lamichhane, to power with an almost two-thirds majority. Former Kathmandu mayor Balendra Shah subsequently became prime minister.
Article Summary: Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 589 foreign nationals, following the flash floods that struck Rasuwa, a district bordering China, and neighbouring areas on August 26. The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayas, unleashing powerful floodwaters that caused widespread loss of life.

Article Title: Witkoff, Kushner reach Kyiv after meeting Putin as Washington steps up Ukraine peace push
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff, left, and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday.

Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready for talks

Moscow meeting ends without major breakthrough

Fighting continues despite diplomatic efforts

Ukrainians remain divided over peace prospects

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reached Kyiv on Sunday for their first official visit to Ukraine, as Washington renewed efforts to find a way to end the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than four years ago.The visit came a day after the two American representatives held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Their trip to Kyiv is part of a renewed diplomatic effort by the Trump administration, even as Russia and Ukraine continue to launch attacks against each other.US efforts to broker an end to the conflict had slowed in recent months, with the Trump administration turning much of its attention towards the war involving Iran.The situation on the battlefield remains difficult. Russia has increasingly used fast-moving, jet-powered drones in its attacks, while Ukrainian forces continue to face Russian troops along a front line stretching about 1,250 kilometres.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was prepared to hold a serious discussion with Witkoff and Kushner.“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed.Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.The two US envoys travelled to Kyiv by train and were received by senior Ukrainian officials at the railway station. They later met Zelenskyy during a ceremony at St Sophia Square.Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, said representatives from Ukraine's European partners, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, were also present in Kyiv.Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday, but neither side announced a major breakthrough after the closed-door discussions.Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov called the talks constructive, frank and useful, but did not reveal any specific agreement or progress.According to Ushakov, Russia presented its “comprehensive assessment” of the military situation in Ukraine. However, the discussions also covered issues beyond the war.“Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail,” he said.Witkoff and Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, had last visited Moscow in January, when they also met Putin at the Kremlin.The diplomatic activity has taken place against the backdrop of continued attacks by both sides.Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause attacks on each other's capitals during the talks. However, officials reported exchanges of fire overnight into Sunday.Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Russian attacks in several regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others.A Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three others. Another drone strike damaged an apartment building in the Khmelnytskyi region and injured seven people.Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted 82 of the 108 drones launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.Russian authorities also reported a Ukrainian drone attack. A man was killed and a woman seriously injured after a drone struck a vehicle in Russia's Belgorod border region.Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences had destroyed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight across 14 Russian regions, Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.The renewed diplomatic activity has brought some hope in Ukraine, although many remain doubtful that it will lead to an immediate end to the fighting.In Kyiv, dozens of people gathered for the daily 9 am moment of silence held across the country to remember Ukrainian soldiers who have died in the war.Among them was 67-year-old Nataliia Lipei, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022. Despite health problems, she has travelled to different cities to take part in the commemorations. She said she hoped the latest meetings would finally help end the conflict.“I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this,” Lipei told The Associated Press.Others were far less optimistic. Oleksandr Pastukhov, a 27-year-old video editor who attended the commemoration, said previous diplomatic efforts had failed to produce lasting results.“We’ve already seen delegations like this come here before,” he said. “We’ve seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we’re supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something.”Pope Leo XIV also renewed his call for peace in Ukraine during his Sunday prayer at the Vatican. He said he hoped the latest diplomatic efforts would lead to meaningful progress.“I hope that the efforts undertaken in recent days to resume negotiations will bear concrete fruit and make way for diplomacy," he told the gathered faithful in St. Peter’s Square at the Vatican.
Article Summary: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrive in Kyiv. Visit comes a day after they held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says country is ready for talks. Russia and Ukraine continue attacks against each other.

Article Title: Meet Kiran Reddy, the 18-year-old Georgia teen who became the first Indian American to win Miss Teen USA
Article Text:
Kiran Reddy makes history just weeks after becoming first Indian American to win Miss Georgia Teen USA

Academic background and roots in Georgia

Cultural impact and upcoming international stage

An 18-year-old student from Douglas, Georgia, has made history by becoming the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. Kiran Reddy defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant, held at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026, according to WALB News and Pageant Circle. Reddy, who had earlier become the first Indian American to win the Miss Georgia Teen USA title, also secured Georgia’s first national victory in the pageant’s history. Her win marks a double milestone for diversity and state representation in the long-running beauty contest.Speaking after her victory, Reddy shared her emotions about taking on the prestigious title. "I am so blessed to represent Georgia and the U.S. and be the role model I always needed growing up," Reddy said, as reported by KFI AM 640. The national finals brought together contestants from all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Raquel Olea of Arkansas was named first runner-up, while Elisa Akin of New York, Kiersten Alvarado of Indiana, and Chloe Bella Dietz of Texas completed the top five. The event was hosted by model Sean Michael Rae and former titleholder Noelia Voigt.Last year’s winner, Mailyn Marsh of Missouri, placed the crown on her successor. The judging panel included notable figures such as Kelsey Swanson, a former Miss Rhode Island USA.Before gaining national attention, Reddy achieved academic success in Coffee County, Georgia. She graduated as the valedictorian of Coffee High School in Douglas. After graduating from high school, Reddy enrolled at the University of Georgia, where she is studying biological sciences on a pre-medical track. Her goal of working in healthcare has been an important part of her platform alongside her pageant career. Reddy’s journey in pageantry has taken years of hard work. She entered competitive pageants at the age of 15. She finished as first runner-up at the Miss Georgia Teen USA contest in 2024, followed by a second runner-up finish in 2025. Her path to the national title began in June 2026, when she was appointed Miss Georgia Teen USA through an open casting call organised by the national pageant organisation, according to reports by WALB and Wikipedia.Reddy’s historic victory highlights the growing representation of Indian Americans in US beauty pageants. As the first Indian American teenager to win the national crown, her achievement has attracted attention from community leaders and pageant fans around the world. Her duties as Miss Teen USA will soon include international representation. Reddy is scheduled to represent the United States at the Miss Teen Universe contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 2026. This will be the first time the national organisation participates in the global event. Along with international travel and official appearances, Reddy plans to continue her undergraduate pre-med studies at the University of Georgia while carrying out her duties as Miss Teen USA. As she steps into the role, Reddy will balance her studies with a year of travel, public appearances and opportunities to advocate for causes close to her heart.
Article Summary: Kiran Reddy, 18, is the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. She defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026. Reddy is scheduled to represent the United States at the Miss Teen Universe contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 20 26.

Article Title: Too many allies? Why Netanyahu's far-right partners are hurting him in upcoming Israel polls
Article Text:
Netanyahu’s far-right allies in Israel are posing biggest challenge for him

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing an unusual threat ahead of the October 27 election: divisions within the far-right bloc that support his government.Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, which ran together in the 2022 elections, have rejected Netanyahu's calls for another merger amid tensions. Meanwhile, smaller parties led by former Likud members and former general Ofer Winter are competing for the same right-wing voters, deepening fragmentation.“When we unite, we win. When we split up, we lose,” Netanyahu told Israel's local media outlet Channel 14, according to AP.Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Friday rebuked national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for refusing to run on a joint slate with finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, warning that a divided vote could weaken the coalition’s chances of retaining power.Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel’s electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.Under Israel’s electoral system, parties must secure at least 3.25 per cent of the vote to win representation in the 120-member Knesset. A party that falls below the threshold receives no seats, making fragmentation particularly consequential for Netanyahu’s bloc.The Financial Times reported that Netanyahu has sparred publicly with Ben-Gvir, who rejected a meeting this week to discuss a merger with Smotrich. Ben-Gvir accused the prime minister of an “attempt to weaken” his Jewish Power party.Netanyahu responded by urging Ben-Gvir to “not burn tens of thousands of rightwing votes . . . and crown a leftwing government”, while also telling him to “overcome your personal ego”.Ben-Gvir, however, argues that a merger could cost his party seats. “According to all the polls, a connection between me and Smotrich distances Jewish Strength by 3-4 mandates who won't come to vote, and the right-wing government will fall!” he wrote on X.The dispute has left Netanyahu pressing harder for unity. In a video posted on X, he said Smotrich and Ben-Gvir “must unite. Every time we ran united, we won. When we ran separately, we lost.”“In 1992, the Right had more votes than the Left, like today, but because we were running separately, we got the disaster of Oslo, Arafat, Hamas and recurring catastrophes,” Netanyahu said, referring to the peace process launched through the Oslo Accords.Smotrich appeared more receptive, writing on X, “It's time for unity and responsibility in the national camp.”Netanyahu subsequently invited Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to meet on Sunday, saying, “We must not waste a single vote; we must unite to save the right-wing bloc!”The stakes are high for Netanyahu, whose nearly uninterrupted 17 years in power are being tested in an election shaped by the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, mass protests and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately.
Article Summary: Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties. The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately. Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel's electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.

Article Title: A 12-foot Burmese python revealed Florida’s bizarre new method for finding hidden invasive snakes after it swallowed a collared opossum
Article Text:
Florida researchers discover a strange new way to track hidden pythons

How a swallowed collar keeps tracking Florida pythons from inside

Why Florida researchers release collared opossums where pythons are hunting

How collared opossums lead Florida researchers to large Burmese pythons

Florida has tried dogs, drones and scout snakes to find hidden pythons

Florida’s unusual python tracker does not always lead to a snake

How Florida researchers adapted their collars to track hidden pythons

Why Florida’s Burmese pythons are a growing concern for native wildlife

Deep in the forests of Florida’s Key Largo, an opossum is being used to find an animal that researchers rarely see coming. Fitted with a small tracking collar and released back into the wild, the marsupial goes about its normal movements through the undergrowth. The collar is programmed to notice when that movement suddenly stops. If the signal later starts travelling again, it can point scientists towards a Burmese python carrying the device inside its body. The unusual method grew out of a mammal-tracking project rather than a plan to hunt snakes.A strange signal in 2022 led researchers to a large female python that had swallowed a collared opossum, revealing that the transmitter could continue working inside the snake. Since then, the approach has been developed into a practical way of locating some of Florida’s largest invasive pythons, which can be exceptionally difficult to spot in the Everglades.As reported by South Florida Sun Sentinel, the idea did not begin as a python-hunting technique. In 2022, Michael Cove, curator of mammals at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences, was studying how raccoons and opossums used Crocodile Lake National Wildlife Refuge.Then one of the collars behaved strangely.A mortality signal indicated that an animal had stopped moving. That might have meant a road accident, an attack by another animal or some other cause of death. But the signal later began travelling again. It stopped, moved, stopped again.That pattern was difficult to explain if the collar was still attached to the opossum. It made much more sense if the animal had been eaten and the collar had remained inside its predator. The likely culprit was a Burmese python.Tracking the signal was not straightforward. Key Largo is built on ancient coral rock, with a landscape containing holes, cavities and places where a large snake can remain concealed. It took about a month before the team located the animal responsible.They eventually recovered a female python measuring about 12 feet long and weighing roughly 66 pounds. It had egg follicles, indicating that it was a reproductive female. The collar was still intact inside the snake and transmitting a signal.Burmese pythons have a useful weakness from the perspective of the tracking system: they digest large meals slowly.A collar swallowed with an opossum does not immediately disappear. Instead, it remains inside the python while the snake digests its meal. That gives researchers time to follow the signal.The important sequence is the change in behaviour. A collar first reports that its animal has stopped moving. Later, the signal itself starts appearing in different locations. For biologists, that combination can indicate that the opossum has been eaten and that the predator carrying the collar has moved.The team began developing the accidental discovery into a more deliberate method. Grant support from the South Florida Water Management District helped turn the experiment into a larger field operation, while Southern Illinois University graduate researcher A.J. Sanjar became involved in working out how the technique could be used more effectively.According to the Washington Times, the equipment also became cheaper. Early collars could cost around $1,500. Later versions were available for about $190, making it much easier to consider fitting larger numbers of animals.The opossums are deliberately fitted with collars because they are potential prey for Burmese pythons. After being captured, however, they are returned to the same habitat rather than moved somewhere unfamiliar.That distinction matters to the researchers because the animals would still be exposed to predators, vehicles and other hazards in the wild. The collar allows the team to learn what happens when one disappears.According to CBS12 News, Jeremy Dixon, manager of the wildlife refuge, has defended the approach by pointing out that the danger faced by the opossums already exists. The research is intended to reveal when one has been taken by a python and use that event to locate the snake.Still, the method raises an obvious question: does fitting an animal with tracking equipment and releasing it as a potential meal amount to deliberately putting it in danger? There is no simple way around that question. The project depends on a predator eating the very animal carrying the device.The choice of opossums has another advantage. A large Burmese python can swallow a surprisingly substantial meal, while a smaller snake cannot. A collared opossum therefore works, in effect, as a size filter. The system is more likely to lead researchers towards a python capable of consuming it.That is useful because large females are particularly important targets. Burmese pythons can produce large numbers of eggs, so removing a mature female can prevent a substantial number of young snakes from entering the population.By April 2026, the project had been credited with helping locate and remove 18 Burmese pythons. Every one was more than eight feet long, with the largest measuring around 13 feet.Dixon said, “These are all reproductively viable pythons.”At that stage, 32 opossums had been fitted with collars, with the team aiming to increase that number to at least 40 during the summer.One python apparently provided an especially clear demonstration of how the system could work. A 12-foot snake was found to have swallowed two collared opossums, producing two separate mortality signals from essentially the same location.The opossum system sits within a much larger effort to locate Burmese pythons, which have become firmly established across southern Florida.Finding them is difficult because the snakes are well camouflaged and can remain out of sight for long periods. Researchers and wildlife managers have consequently tried several different approaches, including detector dogs, drones, thermal imaging and specially trained male pythons that can act as scouts. There have even been attempts involving robotic prey.The difficulty is partly a matter of scale. The Everglades contains vast stretches of wetland, forest and difficult terrain, much of it unsuitable for people searching on foot. A python does not need to move far or make much noise to avoid being detected.That makes an animal which naturally travels through the same habitat an intriguing tracking device.The method is far from foolproof. In one case, a collar produced the expected mortality signal before beginning to move again. Researchers followed it, expecting to find a python. Instead, they encountered fresh snake faeces and the collar.The python had apparently swallowed the opossum, retained the collar long enough for it to transmit and then passed the device. By the time researchers arrived, the snake had gone.There have also been collars that simply disappeared. At one stage, three of 43 deployed collars were confirmed to have been eaten, while six could no longer be located. So the signal does not always end with a captured python. Sometimes it becomes a trail that goes cold.The equipment has also changed as the researchers learned what information they actually needed.The early approach relied on GPS movement data. But once the basic trick was understood, detailed movement histories were less important. The key requirement was knowing where the collar was when researchers needed to find it.By 2026, the project had moved towards simpler VHF transmitters rather than full GPS tracking. Their batteries could last close to two years, reducing the amount of maintenance required in the field.The collar does not need to tell researchers everywhere a snake has travelled. It only needs to remain inside the snake long enough to point towards it.The research published in PNAS, titled ‘ Severe mammal declines coincide with proliferation of invasive Burmese pythons in Everglades National Park ’ revealed that Burmese pythons have had particularly severe effects on native mammals in the Everglades. A long-running road survey published in 2012 recorded dramatic declines in sightings of several species inside Everglades National Park, including raccoons, opossums and bobcats. Opossum observations fell by 98.9% in the survey, while raccoon sightings declined by 99.3%.Those figures should not be read as a statewide population census. They came from a specific road survey within the national park. Even so, the scale of the recorded change illustrates the ecological pressure associated with the spread of the snakes.The US Geological Survey has also documented substantial impacts from invasive pythons on native wildlife in south Florida.Against that background, the collared-opossum experiment is less about finding a clever gadget and more about solving a basic problem: how do you locate an animal that is exceptionally good at remaining unseen?For the researchers, the answer has turned out to involve another animal moving through the same landscape. An opossum walks into the forest with a transmitter around its neck. Somewhere out there, a python may be watching.
Article Summary: Florida researchers are using opossums to track Burmese pythons in the Everglades. The collars are fitted to the marsupial and it is released back into the wild. When it stops moving, the collar sends a signal to a nearby python. The collar remains inside the python while the snake digests its meal.

Article Title: California turned a dirt lot beside Highway 41 into a $1.6M garden with 18 planting beds, murals, and space to grow food
Article Text:
Pic credit: ERIC PAUL ZAMORA

Former dirt lot gets a colourful new life

Pic credit: ERIC PAUL ZAMORA

Who gets to garden

Pic credit: ERIC PAUL ZAMORA

Pic credit: ERIC PAUL ZAMORA

A former dirt lot situated near Freeway 41 and McKinley Avenue has got a new purpose, a greener one. The dirt lot, which sat neglected for years, was transformed last week into a garden called the McKinley Peace Garden, where neighbours can grow tomatoes, herbs, or whatever (legal crops, of course) they choose, Fresnobee reported. The $1.6 million transformation was funded by the state's Caltrans agency, as part of the Clean CA Program, a $1.1 billion effort to enhance communities and clean up roadsides. On Friday, September 4, the garden was opened with a ribbon-cutting that drew local, state, and federal officials.Caltrans worked with the city and several nonprofit organisations and decided to repurpose the vacant land that sits between the southbound Freeway 41 on-ramp and McKinley Avenue. Eighteen concrete planting beds now sit where dirt used to accumulate trash. An open-air, barn-style shelter provides shade. Two murals by artists Erica Thomas and Vanessa Gomez are featured on the iron fence that protects the garden.
