There's even a bathroom and storage, details that matter more than they sound when you're building something meant to last.“It’s taking advantage of an underutilised space within our community, turning it into something very, very beautiful, and that’s what we have here today, right here in the heart of our city,” Fresno Mayor Jerry Dyer said.He added that the project mirrors what the city has done with its Beautify Fresno campaign. “And that is to beautify spaces in our community, to restore curb appeal and to restore neighbourhood pride, and that’s what this garden will do.”Fresno residents can use the garden. They can rent a plot for $41 annually, a fee that also covers water. That price point matters because it's accessible, but also signals that the garden isn’t free for all. The ones who care should invest. The city's Parks and Recreation Department will handle upkeep, and staff are already reaching out to households to spread the word. The city is working with Fresno Metro Ministry to contact residents within a one-mile radius of the garden to let them know about the project, Aaron A. Aguirre, Parks and Recreation Department director, said.You don’t necessarily have to be a seasoned gardener to rent a plot here. Even first-time gardening enthusiasts can try, as they provide free workshops, Dyer said.“I know there were people that had reservations about what this was going to look like and whether this was the right spot for this garden. But I think we can all say today, it was a good choice,” he said. In neighbourhoods where food access is fragmented and supermarkets are sparse, this community garden can really be a boon.The ribbon-cutting ceremony was also attended by Rep. Jim Costa, D-Fresno; Assemblymember Dr. Joaquin Arambula, D-Fresno; Michael Navarro, Caltrans District 6 director; Luis Martinez, representing Sen. Anna Caballero, D-Merced; and Councilmember Nelson Esparza.Nelson Esparza appreciated everyone involved in the development of the property, which he said had become somewhat of an eyesore. He pushed for the project and spent time searching for the right name. His mother eventually suggested ‘Peace Garden’, and that stuck. During the ceremony, he also thanked his mother, Brenda Hernandez, for helping him come up with a name for the garden. “What I love about community gardens is that they give people a reason to come outside, and more importantly, to give neighbours a chance to connect,” Esparza said.And just like that, the Peace Garden is open to Fresno residents. A lot that could have remained a dust trap for another decade is now a garden. The residents now have access to soil, sunlight, and the opportunity to grow something. This green space will shortly foster a community of people who deeply care about making a difference and transforming it into a green paradise. Are you a Fresno resident? If yes, do you plan to rent a plot in this beautiful community garden? What would you like to plant? Let us know in the comments below.
Article Summary: The McKinley Peace Garden is a $1.6 million community garden in Fresno, California. Residents can rent a plot for $41 annually, a fee that also covers water. Two murals by artists Erica Thomas and Vanessa Gomez are featured on the iron fence that protects the garden.

Article Title: Meet Benjamin Choi, a 17-year-old who built a $300 mind-controlled prosthetic arm that reads brainwaves through non-invasive electrodes
Article Text: Each one of us spent the pandemic doing something that we normally wouldn't have the time to. While some picked up numerous indoor hobbies, others studied hard enough to change career pathways. Benjamin Choi, a then 17-year-old kid, put his spare time during the phase to design an accessible device that does not require brain surgery.When he was in third grade, Choi watched a "60 Minutes" documentary about a mind-controlled prosthesis. Researchers implanted tiny sensors into the motor cortex of the brain of a patient who moved a robotic arm using her thoughts. “I was really, really amazed at the time because this technology was so impressive,” he said to Smithsonian Magazine. “But I was also alarmed that they require this really risky open brain surgery. And they're so inaccessible, costing in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.”Years later, when the pandemic hit in 2020, Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia found himself with ample free time. The lab in which he’d planned to spend his summer researching aluminium fuels had shut down. But the documentary he had seen years earlier stuck with him, and he decided to use his spare time to build a less-invasive prosthetic arm himself.He formed a makeshift laboratory on the ping-pong table in his basement and designed the first version of his robotic arm using his sister's $75 3D printer and some fishing line. The printer couldn’t build pieces over 4.7 inches in length, so Choi printed the arm in tiny pieces and bolted and rubber-banded it together. In total, it took about 30 hours to print. This version worked using brain wave data and head gestures, and Choi posted instructions online for anyone to build their own.He had some previous experience building robots and coding from participating in competitive robotics at the elementary, middle school and high school levels, even going to the world championships several times. Starting in ninth grade, he taught himself the computer programming languages Python and C++ by watching videos on Stack Overflow, a website for programmers.After more than 75 design iterations, Choi's non-invasive, mind-controlled robotic arm could be made from engineering-grade materials, able to withstand weights up to about four tons. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves. And it only costs around $300 to manufacture—a huge savings compared to what’s currently on the market. A more basic, body-powered upper limb prosthesis costs about $7,000. As of 2015, the very advanced, full-arm Modular Prosthetic Limb, which has 26 joints, hundreds of sensors and can curl up to 45 pounds, cost about $500,000. This prosthesis, paired with a surgery to reroute nerves that once controlled the arm, allows patients to command the limb with their thoughts and even feel texture through it.Choi’s arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. EEG devices record the brain’s electrical activity using sensors placed on the head. They are often used in medicine to diagnose epilepsy or other brain disorders. His system uses two electrodes: a baseline sensor that clips onto the earlobe and another on the forehead that collects EEG data. The forehead electrode picks up brain wave information, which is sent to a microchip in the prosthetic arm via Bluetooth. An A.I. model that Choi created, also embedded in the chip, deciphers the data and converts it into a prediction of what the brain is thinking. The arm also moves using head gestures and stops with intentional blinks.The invention earned Choi a spot in the top 40 finalists of 2022's Regeneron Science Talent Search, America's oldest and most prestigious science and math competition for high school seniors. “It means a lot to me to see that my work is recognised like this,” Choi said at the time. “I'm definitely very grateful to be a finalist.” The young inventor went on to win funding from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2021 to continue his research and work with experts at the university. For about six months, he experimented with cloud computing to make the arm internet-compatible. To create his A.I. model, he worked independently with six adult volunteers for about two hours each, collecting their brain wave data at his school and home. While collecting the data via an electrode on the forehead, he asked each participant to focus on clenching and unclenching their hand. He trained the A.I. to distinguish between the brain signals, and the A.I. model continuously learns from a user’s brain waves. In total, the algorithm has over 23,000 lines of code, with 978 pages of math and seven completely new sub-algorithms. Choi’s algorithm performs with a mean accuracy of 95 per cent. He said the previous gold standard for a similar artificial neural network was 73.8 per cent.In 2021, he was selected as a Simons Fellow at Stony Brook University, where he worked remotely with Ji Liu, a professor in the department of electrical and computer engineering, on the machine learning algorithm of his AI. Choi has also won awards in the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, the Microsoft Imagine Cup, and the National At-Home STEM Competition. He received a manufacturing grant in October 2020 from PolySpectra, Inc. , a company that produces durable 3-D printed materials, to produce his arm.Over the past few years, Choi has only furthered his achievements. In 2023, he did machine learning research at The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. From August to December 2024, he worked as a researcher with NASA and currently works as an AI researcher at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He is about to graduate with a degree in applied math and a concurrent master's in computer science from the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.The bionic arm, whose underlying signal processing he continued developing at Johns Hopkins, was the foundation of Choi’s interests. But his time at SEAS, whether with the Weber Group or Kempner Institute, has both broadened and refined his understanding of machine learning. Now set to enter the workforce, Choi is fully ready to continue what he’s always done: find ways to apply his research in the world around him.
Article Summary: Benjamin Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia, has designed a mind-controlled robotic arm that does not require brain surgery. Choi's arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves.

Article Title: A self-made billionaire couple gave San Francisco State University $25 million in XRP, one of the largest crypto donations to US higher education
Article Text:
PC: San Francisco State University

How did San Francisco State get its first $25 million XRP donation

Image AI generated

The $25 million gift led to a college renaming

Donation launched five new business initiatives

Gift honoured Lyna Lam’s family history

A self-made billionaire couple gave San Francisco State University a $25 million gift, with a large portion of the donation made in XRP, making it one of the biggest cryptocurrency contributions to US higher education at the time. Chris Larsen, an SF State alumnus, and his wife Lyna Lam donated to the Rippleworks Foundation in April 2019. The gift established funds for the university’s College of Business and supported new initiatives focused on innovation, entrepreneurship and financial technology. According to San Francisco State University, the XRP contribution was the institution’s first digital asset donation and ranked among the largest digital asset gifts made to a US university. The donation also led California State University to rename the College of Business the Lam Family College of Business. The couple had supported SF State since 2001, with previous contributions exceeding $800,000 for scholarships, education, science and business initiatives.In April 2019, San Francisco State University President Leslie E. Wong announced the $25 million donation from Chris Larsen, Lyna Lam and the Rippleworks Foundation.The gift established the Chris Larsen and Lyna Lam Funds for the College of Business, intended to strengthen the college’s ability to respond to changes in the business sector. The university said the contribution would also help prepare students for careers as business innovators and entrepreneurs.A large portion of the donation was made in XRP, which the university described as the first digital asset donation in SF State’s history. The gift was also among the largest donations made in digital assets to a US university at the time. The use of XRP distinguished the contribution from conventional university donations made through cash, securities or other traditional assets. At the same time, the funds were directed towards the university’s business education and innovation programmes.The contribution also resulted in the renaming of San Francisco State University’s College of Business. California State University announced that the college would become the Lam Family College of Business in recognition of the Lam-Larsens’ long-term support and generosity. Chris Larsen, who graduated from SF State with a Bachelor of Science degree in 1984, and Lyna Lam had supported the university since 2001.The $25 million contribution was part of the couple's broader record of giving. Larsen and Lam had donated more than $800,000 to scholarships, education, science and business initiatives across the university, in addition to their gifts to the College of Business. Their previous support included the Chris Larsen Scholarship Fund in the Graduate College of Education and funding for initiatives in the Biology Department within the College of Science and Engineering.Part of the donation established the Lam-Larsen Fund for Global Innovation. The fund was created to bring students, faculty, alumni and outside experts together across disciplines to exchange ideas, explore entrepreneurship and work on solutions to practical problems. The university said the programme was intended to encourage global awareness while helping students develop an understanding of innovation and responsible business leadership.The fund supported five new initiatives within the College of Business: the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Initiative, Emerging and Developing Economies Initiative, Financial Technology Initiative, Business and Education Technology Initiative, and Centre for Workforce of the Future. These initiatives were designed to expand opportunities for students and faculty to work across areas including entrepreneurship, financial technology, education technology and workforce development.The university’s account of the donation also links the Lam-Larsen family’s support to Lyna Lam’s family history. The Lam family, including Lyna’s father Quang Lam, left Cambodia after he led his family’s escape from war and genocide. The family spent time in refugee camps in Thailand and the Philippines before immigrating to the United States and settling in the Bay Area. The university said the Lam Family College of Business was named in honour of Lyna’s family at Chris Larsen’s recommendation.The $25 million donation was also a lead gift for SF State’s BOLD Thinking campaign. The campaign was more than 90 per cent funded when the donation was announced. The university said the contribution was intended to support its efforts in business innovation and entrepreneurship, while building on the Lam-Larsens’ previous financial support for scholarships and academic programmes.
Article Summary: Chris Larsen, an SF State alumnus, and his wife Lyna Lam donated to the Rippleworks Foundation in April 2019. The gift established funds for the university’s College of Business and supported new initiatives focused on innovation, entrepreneurship and financial technology. The couple had supported SF State since 2001, with previous contributions exceeding $800,000 for scholarships, education, science and business initiatives.

Article Title: EBay's first full-time employee left the company after its IPO and built a $5.9 billion fortune; he has now donated about $1.2 billion into social-change projects
Article Text:
Jeffrey Skoll. Image Credit: Skoll World Forum

How did eBay’s first full-time employee build a $5.9 billion fortune

eBay Office. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Leaving eBay marked the start of Jeff Skoll’s mission to drive social change

How Jeff Skoll put billions into social-change projects

2017 Skoll World Forum. Image Credit: Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy

Skoll expanded his efforts beyond philanthropy through impact investing

Skoll used filmmaking to raise awareness of major social issues

Jeff Skoll, eBay 's first full-time employee and president, played a crucial role in building the company before leaving after its 1998 public offering. He helped turn an online auction business into one of the defining technology companies of the internet boom, then chose a different path from the one usually associated with billionaires. Today, Forbes estimates his fortune at $5.9 billion, while his charitable Skoll Foundation and Skoll Global Threats Fund have donated about $1.2 billion worldwide over more than two decades. His journey has moved beyond technology, taking him into philanthropy, impact investing and filmmaking. From helping strangers trust one another in online transactions to funding people working on poverty, health and environmental problems, Skoll's story is ultimately about what happened after the fortune was made and what he decided it should be used for.Jeff Skoll's path to extraordinary wealth began with a decision he initially doubted. According to Forbes, he met eBay founder Pierre Omidyar while studying for an MBA at Stanford University. When Omidyar approached him about the idea behind the online marketplace, Skoll was far from convinced before realising that Omidyar had spotted an important opportunity. Skoll joined the company during its early years and became its first full-time employee and president.According to ‘Celebrity Net Worth,’ he helped turn the young online auction site into a more organised business by writing its first business plan and developing its operational framework.He also helped establish the feedback system that allowed buyers and sellers to rate one another. At a time when online shopping was still unfamiliar to many people, this helped create trust between strangers carrying out transactions over the internet. The business grew rapidly. Celebrity Net Worth reports that eBay went public in September 1998, with its shares initially priced at $18 each. By April 1999, the company's market value had climbed to around $25 billion, making both Omidyar and Skoll billionaires.Skoll eventually stepped away from the company he had helped build. As per Forbes, he left eBay in 2001, three years after its IPO. His departure marked the beginning of a second career focused less on building personal wealth and more on addressing problems around the world. That shift was partly shaped by experiences much earlier in his life. According to Celebrity Net Worth, Skoll's father developed cancer when Skoll was a teenager and later expressed regret about not having enough time to pursue his dreams. The experience left a lasting impression on Skoll and influenced the way he thought about the purpose of work and wealth. The idea of ‘tikkun olam,’ a Jewish concept often translated as ‘to heal the world,’ also became an important part of his approach. Rather than simply treating his fortune as an end in itself, Skoll began to view it as a resource that could support people attempting to solve difficult social problems.In 1999, Skoll established the ‘Skoll Foundation,’ which supports people and organisations working on issues including poverty, education, public health and environmental challenges. Celebrity Net Worth reports that the foundation was an early supporter of social entrepreneurship, an approach centred on finding practical and innovative solutions to major problems. The scale of the effort has grown considerably over time. According to Forbes, the Skoll Foundation and the ‘Skoll Global Threats Fund’ have donated about $1.2 billion around the world during more than 20 years of work.The Skoll Foundation has organised the ‘Skoll World Forum’ since 2004. The gathering brings together people from business, government, philanthropy and civil society to discuss social change and the challenges facing communities worldwide. Skoll later expanded his philanthropic interests through the Skoll Global Threats Fund. As per Celebrity Net Worth, the fund focused on risks including climate change, water security, pandemics and nuclear proliferation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Skoll personally donated more than $120 million to help provide medical equipment and testing supplies to underserved countries.Giving money away was not Skoll's only strategy. Celebrity Net Worth reports that he also became involved in impact investing through ‘Capricorn Investment Group’ and ‘The Rise Fund.’ The aim was to direct money towards businesses that could generate financial returns while also producing measurable social or environmental benefits. This reflected a broader belief that capital could be used in more than one way. Instead of separating philanthropy entirely from business, impact investing attempts to support companies whose work may contribute to improvements in areas such as healthcare, education or environmental sustainability. Skoll also publicly joined the ‘Giving Pledge,’ committing to give away the majority of his wealth during his lifetime.Skoll's interest in influencing society eventually took him to Hollywood. In 2004, he founded ‘Participant Media,’ a production company built around films and television projects intended to entertain audiences while drawing attention to important issues. Films associated with Participant Media include ‘An Inconvenient Truth,’ ‘The Help,’ ‘Lincoln,’ ‘Spotlight,’ ‘Roma’ and ‘American Factory.’ The company demonstrated Skoll's belief that storytelling could sometimes reach people in ways that reports, conferences and traditional campaigns could not.According to Forbes, Skoll announced in 2024 that Participant Media would close after two decades of operation. Today, Skoll's $5.9 billion fortune is a reminder of the wealth created during the rise of the internet. But the $1.2 billion donated by his charitable organisations tells that Skoll chose to spend much of the following decades trying to turn wealth, investment and storytelling into tools for wider social change.
Article Summary: Jeff Skoll was eBay's first full-time employee and president. He left the company in 2001, three years after its public offering. His charitable Skoll Foundation and Skoll Global Threats Fund have donated about $1.2 billion worldwide over more than two decades. Skoll also became involved in impact investing through ‘Capricorn Investment Group’

Article Title: A 69,000 sq ft data centre was planned beside Nashville Zoo; 600,000 people signed against it as a clouded leopard cub became the face of the fight to protect wildlife
Article Text:
Representative image

Why Nashville Zoo opposed the data centre

Nearly 600,000 people signed the petition

Nashville Zoo in Tennessee, which opposed plans for a large data centre to be built on property directly beside its grounds.

Clouded leopard cub Mayuree became a symbol of the campaign

Mayuree, a clouded leopard cub born at Nashville Zoo in May 2026, became a symbol of the zoo's campaign against a proposed data centre next door.

The zoo's concerns focused on noise and light

DC BLOX disputed the concerns

The proposed development could be larger than the initial building

Brad Paisley joined the campaign

Nashville imposed a temporary data centre moratorium

The disputed property became the centre of a bigger battle

The data centre has not necessarily been stopped

A proposed 69,000 sq ft data centre beside Nashville Zoo in Nashville, Tennessee, has triggered a huge public campaign, with nearly 600,000 people signing a Change.org petition opposing the development. The project, proposed by digital infrastructure company DC BLOX, has raised concerns at the zoo over potential noise, artificial light and other impacts from round-the-clock data centre operations on vulnerable animals and conservation programmes. A young clouded leopard named Mayuree, born at the zoo in May 2026, became a powerful symbol of the campaign as the zoo urged supporters to oppose the project. The dispute has since moved beyond the petition, with Nashville officials introducing restrictions on large data centres and authorising steps that could allow the city to acquire the disputed property.The proposed development is located at 648 Grassmere Park, immediately adjacent to Nashville Zoo. The initial project application described a single-storey data centre of approximately 69,220 sq ft on a 23.49-acre property. The zoo raised concerns that a facility operating continuously could introduce persistent mechanical noise from cooling equipment and generators, along with artificial lighting and other infrastructure impacts.The zoo argued that such conditions could interfere with animal behaviour, biological rhythms and breeding programmes, particularly for species involved in conservation efforts. It has stressed that the issue is not simply the size of the proposed building but the potential cumulative effect of a large-scale, continuously operating industrial facility next to animal habitats.Nashville Zoo launched its Change.org petition on June 3, 2026, calling on supporters to oppose the proposed development. The campaign quickly gained national attention, passing 400,000 signatures within days and continuing to grow throughout the summer. By late August, the zoo said nearly 600,000 people had signed the petition, while the Change.org page itself showed more than 599,000 verified signatures. The scale of the response turned what began as a local land-use dispute into a much larger public debate over the environmental and conservation implications of data centre development near sensitive facilities.Mayuree was born at Nashville Zoo on May 5, 2026 and became the zoo's 51st clouded leopard born since 1991. The zoo participates in the Association of Zoos and Aquariums' Species Survival Plan for clouded leopards, making successful breeding an important part of its conservation work. Mayuree was also notable because she was the first clouded leopard cub at Nashville Zoo to be co-reared under the programme, combining maternal care with early human socialisation. As the zoo campaigned against the nearby development, photographs and updates about the young cub helped put a face on its concerns about protecting animals and maintaining successful conservation programmes.Nashville Zoo has argued that the proposed data centre could create a very different sound and lighting environment from the one surrounding its existing animal habitats. Data centres require substantial cooling systems and backup power infrastructure, and the zoo has expressed particular concern about continuous operational noise, including sounds produced by cooling equipment and generators. It has also raised concerns about artificial lighting. The zoo's position is that vulnerable animals should not be exposed to potentially disruptive conditions without strong evidence that the impacts can be adequately controlled. Importantly, the zoo's concerns are about potential future impacts. There is no evidence that the proposed DC BLOX facility has already harmed Mayuree or other animals.DC BLOX has defended its proposal and said the project can be designed to control the impacts highlighted by the zoo. The company said it planned to use closed-loop or waterless cooling and would comply with applicable noise and environmental requirements. It also said generators would be positioned away from the zoo and equipped with measures intended to reduce sound, including sound-attenuating enclosures and muffled exhaust systems. The company has argued that some claims about the project have been inaccurate or overstated and that appropriate engineering controls can address concerns about noise, lighting and other potential effects.The 69,000 sq ft figure describes the building in the initial public permit application, but documents and subsequent reporting have raised questions about the longer-term development planned for the property. A geotechnical document reported by the Nashville Scene described a possible three-storey, 40-megawatt data centre along with a substation and associated infrastructure. Nashville Zoo has also said the wider plans could involve substantially more power capacity than the initial facility. These additional elements are important because the debate has focused not only on the footprint of the first building but also on what could ultimately be developed on the 23-acre site.The campaign also received support from country music star Brad Paisley, who publicly backed Nashville Zoo's opposition to the development and encouraged people to sign the petition. His involvement helped bring additional national attention to an issue that had initially centred on a proposed development in south Nashville. The combination of the zoo's conservation concerns, the rapidly growing petition and high-profile supporters helped make the project one of the city's most closely watched development disputes.The controversy eventually prompted direct action from Nashville officials. Mayor Freddie O'Connell issued an executive order directing city departments to examine the potential infrastructure, environmental and community impacts associated with large-scale data centres. Metro Council subsequently approved legislation establishing a temporary moratorium on the acceptance and processing of permits for data-centre developments. The council also adopted new zoning rules addressing data-centre uses and the conditions under which such facilities can operate. The measures reflect wider concerns around the infrastructure requirements of large data centres, including electricity demand, backup generators, fuel storage, cooling systems, substations, noise, lighting, stormwater and 24-hour operations.DC BLOX purchased the roughly 23.49-acre property for about $23 million in July 2026, adding another layer to the dispute. Rather than simply relying on zoning restrictions, Metro Nashville later approved legislation authorising the city to acquire the property through negotiation or condemnation for stated public purposes. Mayor O'Connell approved that legislation in August. The measure does not mean the city has already seized the property, but it gives Nashville a legal mechanism to pursue acquisition of the site.Despite the petition, moratorium and potential acquisition of the property, the future of the project remains unresolved. The legal status of DC BLOX's proposal has become an important part of the dispute, with questions over whether the project could retain certain development rights because of actions taken before the city's new restrictions came into force. That means the nearly 600,000 petition signatures represent enormous public pressure but should not be described as having definitively cancelled the development. The fight has instead evolved into a broader legal and political dispute over land use, data-centre expansion and the protection of Nashville Zoo's conservation work.
Article Summary: Nashville Zoo in Tennessee opposed plans for a large data centre to be built on property directly beside its grounds. The project, proposed by digital infrastructure company DC BLOX, has raised concerns at the zoo over potential noise, artificial light and other impacts. A young clouded leopard named Mayuree became a powerful symbol of the campaign as the zoo urged supporters to oppose the project.

Article Title: In 1912, Alabama monk Brother Joseph Zoettl began recreating landmarks he had mostly never seen; 46 years later, at age 80, he finished the last of 125 miniatures
Article Text:
Alabama monk Brother Joseph Zoettl

From boiler room operator to visionary outsider artist

Architectural creation through recycled materials and postcards

Preservation and heritage status in Alabama

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think that Ave Maria Grotto should receive more attention as a historic site? Yes, it deserves more recognition No, it's well-known enough I'm not familiar with it It is a niche interest 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

In 1912, a Bavarian-born Benedictine monk at St. Bernard Abbey in Cullman, Alabama, began building miniature cement copies of some of the world’s best-known religious sites, using postcards, pieces of marble and donated costume jewellery as his main guides. Brother Joseph Zoettl spent the next 46 years turning a four-acre hillside quarry into the Ave Maria Grotto. He completed his 125th and final model in 1958 at the age of 80, according to historical records held by the Library of Congress and the official Ave Maria Grotto archives. Although Zoettl had visited only six of the places he recreated, he produced detailed models of landmarks including St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome, the Leaning Tower of Pisa, ancient sites in Jerusalem and the Alamo. The four-acre park remains a major folk-art attraction in northern Alabama and welcomes thousands of visitors each year on the active monastery grounds.Born in Landshut, Bavaria, in 1878, Zoettl moved to the United States in 1892 at the age of 14 to join the newly established Benedictine community at St. Bernard Abbey, according to biographical records from the shrine. Zoettl suffered injuries early in life that left him with a physical disability.He was given the job of operating the abbey’s coal-fired power station and water pump house, a demanding role that could keep him working for up to 17 hours a day. During his short breaks, he began making small stone grottos from discarded masonry and furnace slag. His early miniature creations were placed along the abbey’s recreation paths and also sold in the monastery souvenir shop. As his work became larger and more detailed, abbey leaders set aside a former stone quarry on the campus in 1932 for a permanent display. They asked Zoettl to build a central 27-foot stone cave dedicated to the Virgin Mary.With almost no formal training in architecture or sculpture, Zoettl built his models using ordinary Portland cement mixed with donated scrap materials. Visitors and supporters sent materials from around the world, including cold-cream jars, broken teacups, stained-glass pieces, seashells, marbles and old chandelier crystals, according to Roadside Architecture and regional historical reviews. Since he could not afford to travel internationally, Zoettl depended on black-and-white photographs, souvenir postcards and biblical descriptions to create his models. This approach gave the buildings unusual proportions, with their size adjusted to fit the natural stone ledges of the quarry. Among his 125 completed structures are detailed models of the Basilica of Our Lady of Lourdes, the Great Wall of China, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon and Mission San Juan Capistrano in California. Zoettl completed his final work, a model of the Basilica in Lourdes, France, in 1958. He died three years later, in October 1961, at the age of 83, and was buried in the nearby abbey cemetery.The Ave Maria Grotto was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. The listing recognised its cultural importance as a major example of American outsider art and visionary environment construction. The monastic community and specialist preservation workers oversee the maintenance of the four-acre site. Over the years, Alabama’s humid climate has exposed the delicate concrete and glass structures to weather damage, requiring careful restoration. Staff conservators continue to apply protective sealants and repair individual masonry pieces, helping preserve Zoettl’s life’s work in its original stone quarry setting on the St. Bernard Abbey grounds.
Article Summary: Brother Joseph Zoettl spent 46 years turning a four-acre hillside quarry into the Ave Maria Grotto. He used postcards, pieces of marble and donated costume jewellery as his main guides. Among his 125 completed structures are detailed models of the Basilica of Our Lady of Lourdes, the Great Wall of China and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

Article Title: Since 2007, New York's Rockefeller Center Christmas tree has been milled into lumber after the holidays; the wood has helped build Habitat homes from New York to Mississippi
Article Text:
Rockefeller Center Christmas trees has been used in Habitat homes in several communities, including locations in New York, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Mississippi and Maryland.

Rockefeller Center Christmas trees get a second life

Sarah and her daughters plant vegetable seeds in planter boxes made from 2022 Rockefeller Center Christmas tree lumber.

A Christmas tree becomes part of a family home

Poll Vote & Share your view Which year do you think had the most impact based on the lumber donations from the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree? 2007 2017 2022 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

For millions of people, the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree is a familiar part of the holiday season in New York City. Every year, the large tree stands in the plaza, decorated with lights and ornaments, before being taken down after the holidays. But its journey does not end there.Since 2007, lumber from the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree has been donated to Habitat for Humanity for use in housing projects. According to the organisation, the tree is milled into construction material and used to help build or improve Habitat homes.The programme is part of a longstanding partnership between Habitat for Humanity and Tishman Speyer, the owner and operator of Rockefeller Center. Tishman Speyer donates the tree's lumber to Habitat, while company staff members work alongside Habitat families on construction projects.The arrangement has connected a Christmas tradition seen by millions with homes where families can continue creating their own memories. Some homeowners have lumber from Rockefeller Center trees built directly into parts of their homes, making the history of the tree a permanent part of their houses.Rockefeller Center usually selects a Norway Spruce for its annual Christmas display. After the holiday season, the trunk is milled into two-by-four and two-by-six beams. Tishman Speyer then donates the lumber.The wood is particularly useful for several parts of construction. Norway Spruce is more flexible and durable than lumber used for load-bearing walls. This makes it suitable for blocking, which means filling, spacing, joining or reinforcing parts of a frame.The lumber can also be used for flooring, furniture and cabinetry. Over the years, wood from Rockefeller Center Christmas trees has been used in homes in several communities, including locations in New York, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Mississippi and Maryland.Jonathan Reckford, CEO of the organisation, said the partnership gives the Christmas tree a purpose beyond the holiday season.“Tishman Speyer generously donates one of the largest and most widely-recognized Christmas trees to Habitat,” Reckford says. “The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree is a reminder to reflect, be thankful and to remember to give back to others among the hustle and bustle of the holidays. That symbol will live on as part of Habitat homeowners’ lives in their new houses.”The connection is also visible at Habitat's headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia. Several walls there feature exposed lumber from the 2018 Rockefeller Center Christmas tree. The wood carries stamps from different years commemorating the annual tree lighting ceremony.The first year of the programme was 2007. That year's Rockefeller Center tree came from Shelton, Connecticut, and its lumber was used in Habitat homes in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The programme continued through the following years.The 2022 tree became part of Sarah'shome in Corinth, New York. Sarah and the Habitat volunteers used its lumber to build a detached side deck and two planter boxes.Sarah planned to use the deck as a place for her family to grill and spend time together. The planter boxes were used to grow vegetables, with Sarah and her daughters planting sweet pepper and carrot seeds.The wood also became a reminder of Sarah's long path towards homeownership. She said she had spent almost eight years improving her credit and savings before being able to purchase a home.“I worked on getting my credit up and improving my savings for almost eight years to be able to purchase a home,” Sarah says. “My kids can see that if you put effort into something, something will come out of it. I hope my kids gain patience and understanding that things don’t happen right away, that it does take time.”Another homeowner, Lakisha, has lumber from the 2017 Rockefeller Center tree in her New York home. Several exposed pieces in her pantry and cabinets carry a commemorative stamp marking the anniversary of Rockefeller Center's 85th tree lighting.“Every day, it’s a beautiful reminder of how far I’ve come,” Lakisha says. “And that you should never give up on your dreams, no matter what.”The 2025 Rockefeller Center tree came from East Greenbush, New York. Habitat said its lumber will be used in homes in communities to be announced in 2026.The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree tradition itself dates back to 1931, when workers excavating the site put up a 20-foot balsam fir. In 1933, Rockefeller Center made the Christmas tree an annual tradition.
Article Summary: Since 2007, lumber from the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree has been donated to Habitat for Humanity for use in housing projects. The tree is milled into construction material and used to help build or improve Habitat homes. The first year of the programme was 2007. That year's tree came from Shelton, Connecticut, and its lumber was used in homes in Pascagoula, Mississippi.

Article Title: A Scottish clan kept a human skull for centuries because legend said removing it would bring ruin; now scientists are testing the story
Article Text:
A skull, a castle and an old Highland legend

The mysterious skull resurfaced in a box

What can science actually reveal?

The curse is being tested against history

For generations, a human skull linked to a bloody Highland legend was kept within the Grant family, surrounded by a warning that taking it away could spell disaster for the clan. Now, more than six centuries after the events at the heart of the story, forensic experts are examining the remains to find out whether the grisly relic really belongs to the medieval figure described in the legend. The investigation is being led by Grantown Museum in Scotland, which is preparing an exhibition and podcast titled The Legend of the Highland Skull. The museum says the project will explore a story involving forbidden love, powerful Highland clans, murder and a supposed curse.The story centres on what is now Castle Grant in Strathspey. According to the tradition recorded in an 1857 letter, the skull belonged to the head of Clan Comyn, who was allegedly killed during a violent struggle involving the Grants and MacGregors over the stronghold then known as Freuchie Castle.The Grants eventually made the castle their seat, and it became known as Castle Grant. The legend held that the skull was retained as a kind of grim family talisman but with one ominous condition: if it ever left Grant possession, the clan would supposedly lose its lands, influence and standing in Strathspey. That part of the story remains folklore rather than established history. What can be established is that a skull associated with the legend survived into modern times.The relic disappeared from public view for years after the Grant family sold Castle Grant in 1983. It was eventually rediscovered by Lord Reidhaven, a descendant of the Grant chiefs, in a family storeroom. It was reportedly sitting inside a Harrods box alongside something almost as intriguing: a letter dating to 1857.The document had been written by Grigor Stuart, a minister from Kingussie who visited the Countess of Seafield at Castle Grant in October that year. His account described the skull and the story that had grown around it, including the claim that it was the remains of the last Comyn associated with Freuchie. Rather than allowing the mystery to remain a family story, Reidhaven brought the skull and letter to Dan Cottam, curator of Grantown Museum. That decision has now turned a centuries-old legend into a forensic investigation.The skull is being examined by specialists in human remains and osteology, including Cat Irving, a human-remains conservator associated with Surgeons’ Hall Museums in Edinburgh. The first examination has already raised fresh questions. The skull appears to have been deliberately sawn across the forehead, with a metal hinge and hook attached to it, effectively turning part of the skull into a container.Researchers are working to establish basic facts that could either support or challenge the traditional account, including whether the remains belonged to a man or woman, the person’s approximate age, and any evidence of injury or disease. Most importantly, determining the skull’s age and comparing the physical evidence with the historical account will be crucial to assessing whether the story holds up.The timing is particularly striking. The skull has now left the possession of the Grant family, precisely the act the legend warned would bring about the clan’s downfall. But this time, the purpose is not to test the curse.Grantown Museum is using the investigation to examine how stories survive, change and acquire authority as they pass from one generation to another. The project combines historical research, forensic examination and storytelling rather than treating the supernatural element as established fact.The museum’s Legend of the Highland Skull project includes a four-part podcast, an animated short film and an exhibition. The exhibition is scheduled to run at Grantown Museum from September 7 to October 31, 2026, while the podcast began releasing episodes in September. And after roughly 600 years of legend, one question finally has a chance of being answered: whose skull is it really?
Article Summary: The skull belonged to the head of Clan Comyn, who was allegedly killed during a violent struggle involving the Grants and MacGregors. The relic disappeared from public view for years after the Grant family sold Castle Grant in 1983. It was eventually rediscovered by Lord Reidhaven, a descendant of the Grant chiefs, in a family storeroom.

Article Title: In 2000, NOAA planted 500 square metres of cordgrass and added oyster shell on Pivers Island; the shell mound grew into a living oyster reef
Article Text:
Image AI generated

What happened to the oyster-shell reef

Image AI generated

What did Hurricane Irene reveal about the living shoreline

How did Pivers Island’s shoreline respond to Hurricane Florence

In 2000, NOAA began transforming an eroding stretch of shoreline on Pivers Island, North Carolina, by planting about 500 square metres of smooth cordgrass and placing oyster shell offshore. The project created a living shoreline designed to stabilise the coast while maintaining the natural connection between the marsh and nearby waters. Over time, the planted Spartina alterniflora spread and the oyster-shell mound developed into a live reef, turning the once-eroding beach into an established marsh habitat. The shoreline later faced two major tests from North Carolina hurricanes: Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Florence in 2018. As per NOAA assessments, the following provides a record of how the living shoreline performed during major hurricane events. The Pivers Island project also became part of longer-term research into living shorelines, including their ability to reduce erosion, support coastal habitats and accumulate sediment. Its development offers a documented case of a planted marsh and oyster reef repeated hurricane impacts.The planted cordgrass became the marsh component of the shoreline, while the oyster shell was positioned offshore. NOAA's description states that the oyster reefs increased in height and developed into a living reef, while the planted marsh progressed seaward as sediment accumulated. The site also developed into habitat for fish and birds, while sediment trapped by the marsh contributed to improved water quality.According to the study published in PLOS ONE titled ‘ Living Shorelines: Coastal Resilience with a Blue Carbon Benefit ’, the Pivers Island East marsh was one of two transplanted sites created as living shoreline projects on Pivers Island. The study records that the oyster-shell mound placed offshore had developed into a live reef, while the planted Spartina alterniflora marsh remained part of the shoreline system. The researchers also reported that living shorelines preserve connections between upland and nearshore habitats and can provide erosion control and habitat functions associated with natural wetlands.The first major documented hurricane test came in August 2011, when Hurricane Irene passed directly over Pivers Island. NOAA's assessment examined three shoreline sites, including the Pivers Island East marsh and oyster reef. The report states that Irene provided an opportunity to examine how the vegetated shorelines would perform under hurricane conditions.According to NOAA's assessment, the living shoreline sites experienced substantially less erosion than nearby hardened shorelines during the storm. NOAA's wider project record states that the living shoreline on the Centre for Coastal Fisheries and Habitat Research campus survived the direct impact of Hurricane Irene. The assessment also found that marshes with oyster reefs or other shoreline protection could trap sediment and maintain the shoreline during periods of high wind and wave action.A second major test came in September 2018, when Hurricane Florence affected the North Carolina coast. NOAA's Pivers Island living shoreline record includes before-and-after imagery showing the site before Florence and nine days after the hurricane struck. The images document the condition of the living shoreline following the storm.The NOAA Habitat Blueprint indicates that the site has performed well and that the lawn was eliminated. It also records that the marsh progressed seaward as sediment accumulated and that the oyster reefs increased in height and developed into a living reef. The Pivers Island project therefore provides a documented example of a shoreline established with cordgrass and oyster shell that remained in place through major hurricane events in 2011 and 2018.
Article Summary: In 2000, NOAA began transforming an eroding stretch of shoreline on Pivers Island, North Carolina, by planting 500 square metres of smooth cordgrass and placing oyster shell offshore. The project created a living shoreline designed to stabilise the coast while maintaining the natural connection between the marsh and nearby waters. The shoreline later faced two major tests from North Carolina hurricanes: Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Florence in 2018.

Article Title: In 1929, Louisiana's Oleander Hotel opened on hurricane-prone Grand Isle; 97 years later, residents raised $400,000 to save the island's last historic hotel and turn it into a museum
Article Text:
The organization is developing a comprehensive master plan that will determine how the building can be restored, adapted and maintained over the long term.

A new life for the Oleander

Community support remains crucial

Preserving Grand Isle's identity

On an island shaped by storms, tides and generations of coastal life, one old hotel is getting a chance to tell its story all over again. According to an online report by Houma Times, the historic Oleander Hotel on Louisiana's Grand Isle is being restored nearly a century after it first opened its doors. Restore Grand Isle, the organization leading the effort, wants to transform the landmark into the Grand Isle Cultural Center, giving the historic structure a new role as a visitor center, community gathering place and museum, states the online report. The community has already raised about $400,000 toward saving the building, adds the report. It is reported that the Oleander opened in 1929, becoming part of Grand Isle's history as the island developed as a coastal resort community. Over the decades, Grand Isle became known for its fishing and maritime traditions as well as its unique coastal environment. The Oleander remained a tangible connection to that past, but years of exposure to the harsh Gulf Coast environment left the historic building in need of significant rehabilitation. Restore Grand Isle has now completed initial stabilization work, an important step toward protecting the structure while plans for its future take shape.The organization is developing a comprehensive master plan that will determine how the building can be restored, adapted and maintained over the long term. The proposed Grand Isle Cultural Center would combine preservation with public use. Exhibits would explore the island's fishing and maritime heritage, its history as a destination for visitors and the natural environment that surrounds it. The restored building could also host educational programs, community meetings, cultural events and other activities. Rather than preserving the Oleander simply as an old building, the project aims to make it an active part of island life.While stabilization has been completed, substantial work remains before the Oleander can open as a public cultural center. Restore Grand Isle is seeking additional support from residents, businesses, visitors and people with connections to the island. Donations will help fund continued restoration and rehabilitation while moving the cultural-center plans toward reality. The fundraising effort follows the community's earlier success in raising roughly $400,000, demonstrating the local interest in preserving the landmark.For Grand Isle, the project represents more than the rehabilitation of a historic structure. The Oleander offers a physical link to generations of island residents and visitors who helped shape the community. Its proposed transformation would allow that history to remain part of Grand Isle's future. If the restoration succeeds, the nearly century-old hotel could once again welcome people through its doors, this time not simply as guests of a coastal resort, but as visitors learning about the people, culture and natural landscape that make Grand Isle unique.Image Courtesy: Houma Times
Article Summary: The historic Oleander Hotel on Louisiana's Grand Isle is being restored nearly a century after it first opened its doors. Restore Grand Isle, the organization leading the effort, wants to transform the landmark into the Grand Isle Cultural Center. The community has already raised about $400,000 toward saving the building.

Article Title: Meet Bradley Carlisle, the first professional Santa Claus with Down syndrome in the US: This suburban Atlanta man feared Santa as a child, and now he is honoured by the International Santa Claus Hall
Article Text:
He feared Santa as a child

Bradley Carlisle, a 37-year-old community theatre actor from suburban Atlanta, has become the first professional Santa Claus in the US with Down syndrome. He was also inducted as an honorary member of the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame after completing one of the largest Christmas performer schools in the US in late August. From fearing Santa Claus to embodying him is less a redemption arc and more a reminder about who gets to see themselves in the stories we tell!Bradley Carlisle spent most of his childhood terrified of Santa Claus, according to his mother, Debbie Chadrix, The Guardian reported. He feared St Nick’s white gloves and equated them with the gloves worn by healthcare workers. The medical experiences were difficult for him, and white gloves only meant pain. So when Christmas came around, there was no sitting on Santa's lap, no whispered wishes, no magic.It started in 2023 when Carlisle's mother attended a holiday party thrown by the Down Syndrome Association of Atlanta (DSAA). That’s when the organisation's executive director pulled her aside and said, “We need a Santa with Down syndrome who looks like the kids.”The group’s leader wanted to see if Carlisle would be interested, as they knew his passion for acting. However, she wasn’t sure because she knew her child was terrified of Santa Claus. But she accepted the offer and decided to give it a try. That December, he put on the red suit and showed up. There were more than 200 children.Chadrix can never forget the look on the faces of the children “when they realised Bradley looked like them – and talked like them, a little bit, too”.That’s exactly when Carlisle decided he wanted to be a Santa from then on.By his second Christmas season, the local media picked up Carlisle’s story. His popularity grew. A podcast appearance led to an invitation from Rick Rosenthal, who runs Atlanta's Northern Lights Santa Academy. Rosenthal saw something that others didn’t. It is the second-largest academy of its kind in the US, where actors train to play Santa, Mrs Claus and Christmas elves. When Carlisle arrived at the academy in late August, he trained alongside every other student in the programme. He received no special treatment. At the academy, he learned how to maintain his beard, dress the part and handle the impossible questions kids ask. He excelled in everything.On the academy's final day, Carlisle received word of his induction into the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. Phil Wenz, representing the Santa Claus Oath Foundation, called him to the stage. Carlisle was appreciated for his confident style while personifying Santa Claus. When Carlisle held up the badge, smiling as the audience applauded, it sent a message to the families watching: their kids can do anything. They can even be Santa! Members of the broader Santa community had pooled resources to create a custom-made suit just for him. His photograph will appear in Times Square as part of Down Syndrome Awareness Month, which starts on his birthday, October 1.Carlisle was honoured not just because he has Down syndrome, but because he is a talented Santa who can connect with people with Down syndrome in a way many other Santas may not be able to. And that’s really important. Because on a December evening, a child with Down syndrome will see a Santa who understands them in a way most Santas cannot.When the academy shared plans to welcome Carlisle to the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame, she had one request. She didn't want her son's condition to be the only reason for the honour. She wanted it to be clear that he had earned this place on his merits.“Phil Wenz knows what he’s looking at. And as soon as he saw Bradley as Santa and talking to people and interacting, he knew he had something different and special – and that’s why he got to the Hall of Fame,” she recalled.Down syndrome is part of the story, but not the entire story.
Article Summary: Bradley Carlisle, 37, is the first professional Santa Claus in the US with Down syndrome. He feared St Nick’s white gloves and equated them with the gloves worn by healthcare workers. He was inducted as an honorary member of the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. His photograph will appear in Times Square as part of Down Syndrome Awareness Month.

Article Title: Balochistan’s Zehri under curfew: Civilian killings, detentions and disappearances; what we know
Article Text:
Pakistan's enforced disappearance crisis deepens as four reported missing in Balochistan. Photo credit: ANI

Earlier allegations and UN concerns

A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties.According to a report by The Balochistan Post, Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. Quoting sources,news agency ANI reported that a woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water, while another woman and a man were wounded.Mobile phone services have reportedly been suspended across Zehri, while residents face restrictions on movement. The Balochistan Post said the area has remained under curfew for months, with residents allowed to leave only during designated hours to purchase essential goods. Travel outside the area reportedly requires authorisation from security forces.The Post also reported that Pakistani forces had allegedly killed more than 20 civilians during an operation in the Sohanda area while the curfew was in force.The latest allegations follow a series of reported enforced disappearances elsewhere in Balochistan.On September 2, the local media reported that four people had allegedly gone missing after being detained in Quetta and Dera Bugti, while four previously reported missing persons were recovered from Karachi, Quetta and Hyderabad.The issue has also drawn concern from UN human rights experts. On Saturday, the Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) raised concerns over the alleged enforced disappearance, torture and extrajudicial killing of Imran Ali.The UN experts said Ali was abducted from his apartment on August 27, 2025, by around 20 personnel from Pakistan’s Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). They said people previously detained with him later confirmed that he had been held and allegedly tortured.A police officer reportedly told Pakistan’s Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances in August 2026 that Ali had been killed during an alleged encounter in May. The UN experts called for an independent investigation, forensic examination and identification of six other bodies reportedly brought to a hospital alongside his remains.Meanwhile, Pakistan’s military said on Friday that its forces had killed 48 militants in raids across Mastung, Sibi, Quetta and Kalat over 72 hours, describing those killed as “Khawarij” and “terrorists” without providing evidence, AP reported.
Article Summary: A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties. Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. A woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water.

Article Title: ‘Growing differences between military, Asif Zardari’: Self-exiled Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain makes big claim
Article Text:
Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain (File photo)

Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari , warning that a debate over creating new provinces could push the country into a major political and security crisis.The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, which could include provisions for the creation of new provinces.“Discussions on the creation of new provinces have been raised by interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and DG-ISPR. The proposed constitutional changes reflect growing differences between President Asif Ali Zardari and the military leadership. A political deadlock could lead to serious constitutional consequences, including the imposition of martial law or the formation of an interim government,” Hussain said in a TikTok message on September 2.Referring to the earlier 26th and 27th Amendments, he alleged that political parties had previously reached agreements to facilitate their passage.Hussain also questioned the prolonged foreign stay of Zardari, the husband of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and father of ex-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari."The President had travelled to Austria in connection for his son Bilawal Zardari’s wedding and is currently in London. There was also an hour-long meeting between Zardari and Naqvi in London, claiming that an important message was conveyed to the President," he added.Hussain further cautioned that tensions between the Pakistan military and Sindhi nationalist groups could escalate into widespread unrest. Referring to the situation in Balochistan, Hussain said violence between security forces and Baloch fighters was continuing and called for greater political consideration for the Baloch people.He warned that if Pakistan descended into a broader civil conflict, foreign powers, including the US and UK, would not come to its rescue, and urged Pakistanis to heed his warnings.
Article Summary: Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari. The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:
The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
Article Summary: Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail. Reports allege prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family. His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022.

Article Title: Pakistan: Imran Khan's sister files fresh contempt plea over denied jail visits
Article Text: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan on Wednesday filed a fresh contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court, alleging non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court.In her petition, Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig, as respondents.According to the Express Tribune, the petition was filed after the Supreme Court's August 18 instructions, which mandated virtual communication between Imran Khan and his sons, alongside weekly access for his sisters, failed to materialise.The plea said that Uzma Khan was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday and noted that audio communication with his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition alleged that authorities neglected to establish the necessary infrastructure enabling bi-weekly telephone calls with his sons, Kasim Khan and Sulaiman Khan, as previously ordered by the bench.Earlier, Uzma had filed another contempt application addressing government non-compliance regarding a separate instruction within the August 18 order, which directed that Imran Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital for medical care.Under the original August 18 decision, the Supreme Court instructed that the former premier be transferred to Shifa International Hospital for clinical evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical panel while simultaneously granting visitation rights.Following the orders, authorities transferred Imran Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21. He was, however, sent back to Adiala Jail shortly after medical personnel declared him to be "medically fit".Reacting to the developments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) lambasted prison administrators for barring relatives from seeing the party founder, characterising the restrictions as a flagrant breach of mandates issued by both the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court, as reported by another Pakistan-based daily, Dawn.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan has filed a contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court. She alleges non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court. Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig as respondents.

Article Title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
Article Text:
Indus Waters treaty representational image

India rejects tribunal ruling

Water, terrorism and the SCO

NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.The dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.
Article Summary: Pakistan urges New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty. India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.

Article Title: Leadership gaps cloud Pakistan's human rights oversight system
Article Text:
Pakistan human rights faces pending vacancy

NCHR’s legal status under question

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for an effective human rights body? Strong leadership Independence Transparency Accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty as key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership, raising concerns over their independence and effectiveness.The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025, but a new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report. The National Commission on the Status of Women (NCSW) is also functioning under an acting chairperson.Former NCHR chairperson Khawar Mumtaz criticised and warned that prolonged reliance on temporary arrangements could weaken the autonomy and performance of independent rights bodies.Human rights activist Peter Jacob said Parliament passed legislation establishing the National Commission for Minorities Rights in December 2025, but appointments to the body remain incomplete.The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has also faced vacancies. The Ministry of Human Rights invited applications in July 2026 for members representing Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, The Express Tribune reported.An amendment to the National Commission for Human Rights Act in 2026 introduced Section 4A, allowing a chairperson to continue for up to 120 days after the expiry of their term or until a successor is appointed.NCHR Chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha maintained that the commission remains operationally effective, pointing to additional staff recruited two years ago. She said the extension of the chairperson’s tenure was made under the law and reflected practices followed by human rights institutions internationally. Questions regarding the constitution of a new commission, she said, should be directed to the government, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty. Key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership. The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025. A new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules.
